F1, 81). The faculties granted by Pius IX were, however, subject to the permission of the “respective Bishops and Ordinaries”. Little Chapel. It is not known in which of the four houses opened in Rome; perhaps Tor de' Specchi, the first House opened in Rome.

3 The work had continued to function normally despite the loss of support.

4 The houses are twelve, in order of opening: Mother House, Sampierdarena, Piacenza (Boys' School and Infirmary), Genoa, Ferrara, Nizza Monferrato, Ovada, Foligno, Rome (four).

She explains what linen to bring. For her coming to Rome she should proceed as follows: keep everything in order and leave as soon as she receives the telegram; but if Fr Santi is visiting the house, she is not to move until he has gone. Some advice about the girls.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. I am answering yours, received a few hours ago, in which you tell me you have received mine and all the tickets etc.. You ask which tablecloths to bring: only two of ours, you know, from our refectory, the fringed ones, but not too long, just two; as for napkins, you can bring 4 cotton ones of the arengo(?) cotton kind, and the others from our refectory; towels, just a few, 6. Sheets as I told you.

  2. I didn't understand at all where that person is; I thought in Cremona... enough.2 Listen: today I had a dog's day over that person's affairs; how many enemies he has! I thought I would burst with grief, my God!3

  3. You ask what to do about Father Santi. If he has not yet come, lock up and off you go; come anyway; leave instructions with Buon Pastore, and what the portress is to say; if they are questioned, silence; and if he asks how many nuns we are, a large number; for charity's sake, do you understand me?4

  4. Have more postulants arrived? For charity's sake, don't give Buon Pastore the sheets from the linen room; keep them apart.5 I think your room would be better if your bed too had curtains; see whether you can arrange it.

  5. I hear about the girls; all is well, except the Cesena girls: remember their mother is wicked and would lead them into sin the moment she had them in her power, for charity's sake! Giuseppa Valle yes, but the two Cesena girls must be kept, with patience; likewise the Angel of Paradise.6 Warn Scopesi that she can no longer be kept; but don't send her away, if it can be avoided. «My God! send providence, and then we won't send them away».7

  6. So, have you understood? In any case, as soon as you get a telegram, come. If the telegram comes while you are busy with Father Santi, wait before coming; you all wait, and when Father Santi has gone you will all come together. Have you understood me?

  7. Why do you tell me you don't do all the washing? I think it would be good to do all of it, so you can still see how things are going; don't worry if you can't.

  8. See that Gazzola goes to the country.8 Everything else in person. Goodbye. You will have understood about Father Santi: if he is with you when the telegram arrives, wait until he leaves, then come.

Goodbye. In haste and standing up, I am your

Affectionate Mother. Bring two metres more of scotto besides what is needed for the clothing.9

1 The date is incomplete, but it is certainly April 1873.

2 Fr Tornatore.

3 She had evidently asked some Prelate that he be reinstated at least as director of the two Houses in Piacenza (cf. L 89, 3,5) and had discovered such hostility towards him that it caused her great suffering.

4 Fr Santi (cf. L 11, n. 3) was to visit the Mother House again. Lock up refers to cupboards and rooms. Note the precise instructions: she leaves Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore Dosi in charge of the house, explains how the portress is to answer any questions about the Superior's absence, and suggests explaining to the others how to behave and answer.

5 This Sister was ill.

6 Sr. A. Francesca was reducing the number of girls. The Mother alerts her about some of them. The Angel of Paradise is surely a very good little girl.

7 Adele Scopesi contributed to her daughter's keep. She was to be warned to pay, but the girl was not to be sent away. The Mother ends these painful remarks with an invocation to God and an urgent plea: send providence, and the doors of the house will not open to send them away.

8 For Maria Gazzola, one of the first to enter, she was to do her best to send her to the country for a while.

9 Two metres of scotto beyond what is needed for the clothing.

She sends him a letter from Mgr Mariano and, declaring herself resigned to God's will, begs him to help her in her troubles.

Most Reverend Father,

  1. Knowing how much you care for our good, I send you a letter I have just received from Monsignor Mariano; I hope it will be read only by Your Paternity.2

  2. This poor daughter of yours, who has no one else to whom she can unburden herself amid so many tribulations,3 tells you too that she is wholly resigned to God's will.

  3. My Father, my troubles are countless. Ah! for pity's sake help me, as you have already done so often, and one day I hope to tell you some of them.

Bless me and believe me always Your Reverence's

Most humble Sr. Anna Maria Rosa Gattorno

1 This letter falls within the chronological limits of Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist's letter of 23 April 1873.

2 On behalf of the Cardinal Protector Luigi Vannicelli, he informed her that Don Angelo Pacchino had sent him «a defamatory libel» against her and Fr Tornatore and that the Cardinal had written a long letter to Mgr Magnasco, Archbishop of Genoa, so that he might use his authority, if possible, to stop so much scandal and bitterness for the Mother (AFSA, VW1-83).

3 The Father replied on 27 April with a fine, consoling letter: «you must not be distressed», he said among other things, «but leave it to the Advocate. The Lord will defend the innocent and the poor» (ibid.).

She encloses a letter for the confessor. She has received a printed sheet from Don A. Ricchini.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear of the good harmony in the House.2 I enclose two lines for the Confessor; give them to him at once.3

  2. Don Ricchini sent me a sheet (illegible word) with oaths in it, or rather about oaths; what an eccentric! let him be; it amuses him a little, since meanwhile he has nothing to do.4

  3. Tell the nurses to pray that I may obtain my grace. Give me news of mamma.5 Goodbye

your affectionate M.

1 The letter she answers is dated 27 April '73.

2 The community was serene and at peace.

3 The Confessor, recently appointed through Don Accinelli's intervention with the Archbishop, is Don Borgotto. Cf. Accinelli's L of 18 and 22 April.

4 Cf. L91, n. 2.

5 The grace she desired: approval of the Constitutions. Sr. A. Santina was on excellent terms with Signora Adelaide and often visited her.

She wishes to know whether he can grant her a brief audience.

Most Reverend Father,

  1. A thousand apologies if I trouble you again with my writing; being unable to help it, I must turn to the one who is a Father to me. I have just received your esteemed letter and find no word about the Parish Priest of the Fornaci.1

  2. Through the bearer of this note I should like to know whether you could hear me tomorrow for just a moment. If I am a nuisance, please forgive me.

  3. I have placed everything in God's hands and no longer care about anything. I want God's will alone, my Father, and in it I wish to die. Bless this your very poor daughter, who remains with the greatest veneration Your Reverence's

Most humble Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 She turned to him not only about the Rules but also for advice on the Rome houses. Another work had recently begun in Via delle Fornaci, within the parish of «S. Maria delle Fornaci».

She has received her letter and reassures her; she will not write at length, being very busy: she has opened four houses in a short time. She urges the greatest prudence, given the presence in the house of Signora Colomba and the lay teachers.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. Yesterday evening I received your very sorrowful letter about yourself, since you took to heart the letter the Superior here wrote to you.2

  2. Listen: I grant you weren't thinking about what you said, and that your remark about the number of Sisters...; but if the letter had fallen into other hands, and you, not having been warned, had said this to outsiders, it would certainly have harmed the cause; enough, let it be over now, for I am writing in great haste.3

  3. My work has reached its peak — imagine! four houses have been opened in so short a time.4

  4. Now I'll tell you something I want you to do. Give Signora Colomba a room and then let her do as she pleases; only you must forbid her to come to your offices or to talk with the Sisters, and the Sisters and postulants must not let her hear anything at all, because I want her to know nothing, nothing, because...5

  5. Mind you never let yourself be heard saying anything to the Sisters, and they must never be heard asking you anything, nothing, I beg you. Only you should talk with her and,

when you go out, it will be good to take her with you so that she gets out a little and has some air.6

  1. She asks always to confess to this extraordinary confessor and would like to go to the church where he is; well, agree to it. Have her accompanied by Sr. A. Cecilia and the other, Sr. A. Ignazia, of course when it does not disturb the community and on a day convenient to you.7

  2. Then, about the outside teacher: I am writing to Colomba now so that she is not upset, because this teacher has certain books and says she does not believe in the Saints, that is, that the Lord admits no advocates; what a head, my God!8 Be patient, but for charity's sake make sure no one knows these things; I want you not (?) to be discreet. Alas! if this false talk, spoken and seen by this fanatical head, got about, how much harm it would do! Don't confide in her at all. And let the teacher have little or nothing to do with our religious and teachers, especially the young ones.9

Goodbye, I am tired your affectionate M.

God bless all that community and give it peace...

P.S. Tell the teacher in confidence not to give her books to the religious or [to] others; all in silence.10

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. P. Bucciotti's correspondence, especially her letters of 1 and 6 May 1873.

2 Being very busy, the Mother had had Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, Superior of the Tor de' Specchi house, write to her.

3 On hearing that so many houses were opening she had written to the Mother: «there are more houses than religious». Sr. A. Eletta had pointed out how inappropriate this remark was. (Cf. L 27.4.73, AFSA, F35.2).

4 Houses opened in Rome in April 1873: Tor de' Specchi, the Parrocchietta, the Fornaci, Trastevere (Piazza S. Agata, 1).

5 Signora Colomba Grampini (cf. L 47, 2). She advises how to treat her, since she is not a postulant but a guest; so everyone in the house must be very prudent.

6 When you go out, it is good to take her with you.

7 Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini and Ignazia Losi, both experienced Sisters.

8 The «good» Signora Colomba was scandalized by the lay teacher's ideas.

9 I want you not (to speak of it), to be discreet. She evidently omitted the words speak of it; Have little... young ones. The Mother feared the Sisters and the other young teachers might be influenced by the teacher's unorthodox ideas.

10 Probably books not approved by the Church.

She points out that, as regards the advice she asks about the School, it is best to keep to what Don Bernardino has told her.

A.M.F.

Daughter,

  1. I have received your registered letter asking my opinion on what to do about the School, as that holy man Don Bernardino tells you. Oh! the advice of that excellent Priest is far too wise to be refuted by a wretched Servant of the Lord incapable of giving the slightest advice.2

  2. So hold firmly to whatever you receive from this Priest, and you will always be glad of it.

  3. Many greetings to Signora Biagini3 and to Don Bernardino; I commend myself to his prayers and to those of the Father Guardian,4 while I remain

Your most humble and devoted Sr. Anna Rosa Gattorno

1 The autograph letter lacks addressee and date; both are inferred from the content and the sequence of events. Maria Grampini, a teacher, was keen for the work to succeed.

2 The School had begun to function regularly on 21 April 1873. Only boys were accepted, but very few came, while requests from girls were growing (cf. AFSA, D2). This was a significant problem.. Don Bernardino Palestini, cf. L 29, n. 2.

3 Giovanna Biagini, mother of Caterina, cf. L 85, n. 2, and of Anna Biagini, who entered the Institute in September 1873.

4 The Father Guardian: Fr Giuseppe Sensi OFM.

5 She feels reborn in body and spirit, filled with the tenderness of God, the Shepherd who feeds his flock and gathers it with his arm, carries the lambs in his bosom and gently leads the mother sheep (Is 40:11). The image, of rare beauty and broad pastoral sweep, is taken up and transfigured by her into a vision of lofty spirituality.

6 Three houses: Tor de' Specchi, Fornaci, Parrocchietta. There remains the one in Trastevere, where the community looked after young domestic servants. For that work Sr. A. Del S. Cuore Cocchella seemed suitable to her.

She answers her letter, sorry not to have embraced her again before her departure for Foligno. She is united to her in Jesus: moved by the spirit, she urges her to receive Love and to love Him who wants to be loved.

My Duchess,

  1. I have read your very dear letter. Your words are alive in my mind!1 I would have been only too happy had I had the good fortune to embrace you once more before you left for Foligno! I shall content myself with holding you always in Jesus and seeing you consumed in this fountain of graces.

  2. My dearest, allow me to express myself thus, and cover with the mantle of forgiveness all the expressions you find here. It is the eyes of the spirit, which have no etiquette and know no temporal duty!2 That most pure love desires to come into you; do not refuse him entry, receive him, listen to him. Here, my Duchess, is He who wants to be loved. My God, You alone are... You alone...3

  3. For charity's sake burn these scribbles and forgive me, while I hold you this evening in Jesus to see you again tomorrow at the hour of the Heavenly Table. Forgive your poor little one, who asks it on her knees, while she remains your

Most faithful Servant Sr. Anna M. R. G.

1 «... your letter». Most of the Marchioness's letters (about a hundred in all, 1873–1900 — cf. AFSA, Amiche) are undated or give only day and month. We seem, however, to identify the one the Mother is answering. It is dated 25 April and shows this great woman's sincere and deeply spiritual relationship. Some expressions: «ask the Lord to make me humble... ask for light for me... tell the Lord I would like to be his...».

2 The Mother, deeply touched, looks at her with the eyes of the spirit and speaks with candid expressions free of the human conventions of etiquette; she echoes God's own invitation: «Behold, I stand at the door and knock» (Rev. 3,30).

3 Her message has a strongly prophetic note. The Marchioness replied on 10 May: «Your letter moved me. But what should I answer? Ask the Lord to make me his; I shall try not to resist his grace» (ibid. undated 5).

She is not to speak to the Superiors about money. She is to send the copy of the Rules and give news of her journey.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter,

  1. As for what we discussed about writing to the Superiors for money, don't do it after all; you will hear from me in person that I have thought it over; so say nothing.1

  2. Listen: Sr. A. Vincenza left the Rules in Carlotta's trunk; for charity's sake send them to me at once by registered post; I need them desperately. My daughter, if you knew what I heard today — it's a story to drive one mad.2 Patience! God wills it so, and so be it. How many troubles! I await news of your journey; I am anxious.3 How is Sr. A. Augusta? Give her my warm regards and tell her I always keep her with me.4

Goodbye to you both, and believe me your affectionate M. Rosa

1 During Sr. A. Francesca's stay in Rome they had agreed that she would ask the Superiors for a contribution for the Rome Houses, but the Mother later decided otherwise.

2 ...I need them desperately... to drive one mad. From the tone and words it may be supposed that the incident had occurred which she later told Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, who recorded it in her Appunti della Ven. M. Rosa G.: «I wanted my (Rules) and they answered that they didn't have them and that they weren't there. Do you know what I did? I told them: Look there, up on that shelf, and there they are. Then they had no choice but to give them to me» (cf. AFSA, 80, FCr).

3 She awaits news of her return journey to Piacenza.

4 Sr. A. Augusta Biagini of Foligno had met the Mother during her stay for the foundation of the house. She wanted to follow her and after a period of preparation received the religious habit. The Mother had sent her to the Mother House accompanied by Sr. A. Francesca (cf. L 85, n. 2).

She has no words to express her gratitude for his entrusting to the Daughters of Saint Anne two Schools subsidized by His Holiness. On behalf of the religious and those in their care, she prays that the Lord may fill him with graces.

her Institute, from the first audience on 3 January 1866. She constantly reminded her Daughters of it.

2 The Holy Father gave a monthly subsidy to the Parrocchietta school and the one in Via delle Fornaci.

3 The figure for religious and those in their care is overall and approximate: about two hundred religious and a thousand girls.

Her health is better and she thinks she has identified the cause of her long agony in recent days. She feels at peace and wholly abandoned in God. She asks her to send some Sisters to Rome. She speaks of Fr Tornatore and of her troubles over the approval of the Rules, and tells her of her travel plans in June to visit the communities.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I received your letter, and I had no doubt at all that what I said might not be true.1 Let us leave everything to God; meanwhile let us bless the Eternal Father, and offer prayers of thanksgiving for giving me a little health: for three days I have been completely free of breathlessness, only a slight headache, but nothing to speak of. I am holding up fairly well, I work, and I no longer suffer the painful agony.2

  2. My daughter, now to the point. Listen: I tell you first that this was certainly the cause of my agony: the V. are at it again... do you understand me?3 Something I saw in myself to be wholly God's work, for I did not suffer the slightest disturbance; my God! you will it so, I will it too; and peace spread through me.4

  3. I seem another creature from a fortnight ago. Do, do what you will, my God; I am content and, like a lamb at its mother's breast, I am glad and calm. How good our God is!5

  4. Now another thing: in these days I have put three houses in good order; there remains that of the Servants, and I hope with God's help to do the same there.6 Listen: I thought of making Sr. A. del Sacro Cuore Superior, but I don't know how to bring her here; I shall have Florence written to so that they send you the tickets, and you would have to choose two religious, one to leave in Foligno and the other to come here with Sr. A. del Sacro Cuore. Rack my brains as I may, I couldn't decide whom to choose. See what you think: you have seen what is needed and how we need Sisters who are very reserved, serious, capable and obedient, and of a certain presence.7

  5. Then telegraph Ferrara so that Sr. A. del Sacro Cuore is at Bologna station, and mark their tickets clearly so they can't go wrong. I would like you to do this as soon as possible, so that I can settle them and be free to leave.8

  6. From that person I have not had a single line yet; no doubt he must have received wrongs from me, but returning evil for good is [not] Christian; so, my dear, we must do our part.9 With his blessed maternity he has thrown everything into the air and we are back to the beginning; what do you think? So many troubles! Yet seeing myself so calm consoles me, and in my very suffering I enjoy an indescribable tranquillity.10

  7. If you could be ready to return by 15 June — for I shall stay 15 days in Foligno and another 20 between Ferrara and Bologna — and if the Ferrara Chapel opens for Saint Anne's day, then we shall celebrate the feast, as I hope.11

Goodbye, I am your affectionate Mother Rosa

1 The letter has not survived, so it is impossible to infer what the Mother meant.

2 Let us leave everything to God... bless... offer prayers of thanksgiving. Gratitude to the Father for restoring a little health after the prostrating agony should take shape in the Daughters as a renewed living relationship with him, woven of trust, blessing, praise and thanksgiving.

3 Now that, out of the struggle, she is at peace, she has identified the cause of her illness and reveals it with a brief allusion, veiled by charity, to her trusted Sr. A. Francesca, who knew the facts well: the Vernengo sisters (Sr. A. Concetta and Sr. A. Giuseppa) are again causing ill feeling in the Sampierdarena community. By special concession the second, though ill, had been accepted on the promise that her sister would nurse her. The particular demands of both sisters had created a burdensome situation that periodically erupted in tensions, bad temper and recriminations.

4 Something... God's work. The decision to accept them had seemed good and in keeping with God's will, because their «life annuity» was a real financial help for the poor community.

5 She feels reborn physically and spiritually, filled with the tenderness of God, the Shepherd who feeds his flock, gathers them with his arm, carries the lambs in his bosom and gently leads the mother ewes (Is. 40,11). She takes up this biblical image of rare beauty and broad pastoral sweep and transfigures it into poetry of lofty spirituality.

6 Three houses: Tor de' Specchi, Fornaci, Parrocchietta. There remained the Trastevere house, where the community cared for young domestic servants; Sr. A. Del S. Cuore Cocchella seemed suited to that work.

7 you have seen. Sr. A. Francesca had been in Rome. Cf. L 97.

8 telegraph Ferrara: the Sister was in that community.

9 «Do not repay evil with evil, but on the contrary, repay with a blessing» (1 Pet 3:9).

10 With his blessed maternity. The immaculate maternity of Saint Anne, an expression used by Fr Tornatore in the 1869 Rules, was one of the disputed points: cf. Lettere 2, L 185, n. 4. Evidently it was once again drawing criticism and delaying approval.

11 Work on the Ferrara House was not yet finished. Cf. Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti's correspondence to M. Rosa: AFSA, F30.

She urges her not to be distressed and to be very reserved and discreet in speech. In trial patience is needed; we want our reward from heaven.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Today I sent you a letter and afterwards received a very long one from you. My daughter, courage, for charity's sake, don't be distressed; only listen: for the moment suspend everything, and I shall soon arrive. Keep silent, don't go to the Morte any more, become mute. Perfect silence; speak little; answer only what charity requires: «Yes, no, I don't know; I'll write to the Mother; be a little patient».1

  2. Now I shall have Sr. A. Vincenza write from here to Marquis Landi; it is a time of trial, patience is needed! God suffers tribulations of every kind, so we too, who by his mercy are enlisted under his Banner, must suffer persecution. On the day of judgement we shall see the rich man Dives groan, and poor Lazarus, full of glory, will triumph in the kingdom of heaven.2 Oh! blessed poverty, my dearest Sister! Love her, love her you too.3

  3. As for the rest you tell me, I was very surprised to hear that that person said — that you are a true daughter of your Mother and that we make fun of it — and the other thing you tell me; patience!4

  4. God wills it so; after doing so much and always working under the lash without a word of comfort, here, here is

4

the world's pay! Let us glory in wanting our reward from Heaven, not from earth and all it contains, which is perishable; but the kingdom of heaven knows no decay.5

  1. What can you do about the new mess that has arisen from those...? I must stay here who knows how long yet; patience! everything takes its course.6

  2. Tomorrow I shall write to Don Accinelli to send Sr. A. Lucia and Sr. A. Giacinta; Sr. A. Giacinta will stay in Foligno and Sr. A. Lucia will come to Rome with Sr. A. del Sacro Cuore. There, all neatly done.7

  3. Cheer up, companions, let us drink tasty wine in Jesus' cellar, let us get drunk, let us knock back a glass!8 Anyone can laugh in prosperity, but few know how to be cheerful in adversity. Whoever suffers for Jesus enjoys paradise in advance.9 I think I have nothing else.

Goodbye, I am your affectionate Mother

8. It would be good for you to call on Marchioness Anguissola and give her my regards. That person has so far written me only two lines enclosed with one I was to send to Salù.10 My dear, the world is like this now; stop sending the letters, for charity's sake. I shall come and we shall do everything.

Goodbye, I am your affectionate [Mother Rosa]

1 Since Sr. A. Francesca's letter is missing, all one can tell is that there was some problem in the House in Via della Morte.

2 Marquis Alfonso Landi, friend and benefactor. Expressions full of Gospel spirituality. Cf. Mt 11:12; Jn 15:20; Lk 16:19-21.

3 «My dearest sister»: an expression recalling her Father St Francis of Assisi.

4 Since Sr. A. Francesca's letter is missing, it is not clear what the Father said or in what connection.

5 let us glory: let us count ourselves happy, because we live Jesus' words in the liveliest hope. Cf. Rev 22:12; Mt 5:12.

6 mess... this point too is incomprehensible. Everything takes its course, a Genoese expression.

Don Accinelli: cf. L 2, n. 4. Sr. A. Lucia Faraboli and Sr. A. Giacinta Antoniazzi were in the Genoa community.

8 Cheer up... knock back a glass: an unusual touch to make her Franceschina laugh, so beset by the problems of two houses.

9 The few who know how to be cheerful are those who make the «Beatitudes» their paradise in advance. Cf. Lk 6:20-23; Mt 5:1-11.

10 Marchioness Fanny Visconti di Mondrone. Salù: the word is incomplete; perhaps Saluzzo.

She is surprised that the Sisters from Genoa have not yet arrived. She is in a hurry, needing to organize the community properly as soon as possible so as to carry out her programme: visits to Foligno and Ferrara, return to Piacenza. Various practical instructions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and hear — I can't understand why — that the Sisters from Genoa have not yet reached you; I await them impatiently, for then I would be ready to leave; otherwise who knows how much longer I shall have to stay, since I must leave it well settled and in order; it will certainly take 15 days, another 15 in Foligno and another 15 in Ferrara; I would reach Piacenza in early August, never finishing anything.2

  2. I shall probably have to stop in Perugia; I would like you to give [those] coming to Rome (le) some material to make [an apron], a little cotton cloth, and some cotton or thread to make stockings. I shall probably bring three postulants myself; in the next few days the one from Ovada will reach you; I think she has 500 f. and her outfit. Don't forget the Sacred Heart clock.3

  3. I understood all you tell me about that person: it's the devil sticking his tail in.4

  4. Goodbye for now; I am so tired, having been out all day, and it is already 10 tonight. I am in Trastevere; since yesterday ever more toil. Goodbye, you have done everything well. Greet Sr.

A. Augusta for me. Think about the lottery prizes, to see whether there is a nice one left over to give Mgr Negrotto.5

Goodbye, your affectionate Mother

5. See whether you can send Sr. A. Angelica to Nizza. The Superior asks us to send her, as she badly needs her.6

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 She repeats what she wrote in the previous letters. Cf. L 99, 4. 5. 7; 100,6.

3 She had been to Perugia before to visit the Bishop of the Diocese, Mgr Gioacchino Pecci. Cf. L 52. The postulant from Ovada: Rosa Marchelli. Sacred Heart clock. Cf. L 104,6.

4 That person is Fr Tornatore. Cf. L 2, n. 3.

She warmly urges them to shake off lukewarmness and to serve the sick fervently, for in them is Jesus Crucified. They are to encourage one another in so holy and noble a service.

A.M.F.

My daughters,

  1. Two lines, not of reproach, but drawn from what I feel for you, little short of sorrow; come, shake yourselves, wake from the sleep of lukewarmness into which you have let yourselves sink! My God, how can anyone fall short in the service of that God who is all love for us?1

  2. He, most adorable Heart, never tires of being open to us and calling us to come and be filled with him; he never tires of pouring his graces on us every day. Alas! we tire, or rather we grow languid in serving him in the person of the sick.2

  3. Daughters, before this should happen, pray God to shake you with his grace. Ah! tell his most adorable Heart, in this month dedicated to him, to make you grow in fervour in caring for the poor sick, for in them we see figured his person, the Son of God, Jesus Crucified. What a misfortune it will be for a Daughter of Saint Anne who held the most sublime office of caring for the sick to find herself before his judgement seat, when this most loving Saviour shows her his opened breast and the sufferings he endured for her, because she was indolent in tending him and unwatchful in helping him in his needs!3

  1. And it would be even more dreadful if among these there were any

who go unwillingly; those, I tell you, for whom the Lord's justice will match their conduct; I hope there are none such, for if there were, my heart would break with grief, and I could only call them heartless Daughters, unworthy of Saint Anne.4

5. Encourage one another in so holy and noble a service as caring for the sick. I look forward soon to a letter from you with lively resolutions, all ablaze with charity, to console me.5

Goodbye; I am sorry I cannot go on, as I have to go out. God bless you and make you grow in the way of charity until you are consumed.6 I am your affectionate

Mother Rosa

1 At the beginning of June, the month dedicated to the Sacred Heart, she sends the nursing Sisters a fervent exhortation to serve their sick brothers and sisters in a Gospel spirit (Mt 25:36).

2 The Sacred Heart is always open, constantly inviting us to draw on his love; he never tires of pouring his graces on us daily. But we tire and so grow languid in serving him in the person of the sick.

3 Having indicated the source and purpose of service to others, she traces clearly, in an eschatological key, the spirituality of the Sisters called to the most sublime office of caring for the sick.

4 Those who go unwillingly to care for the sick are unworthy to be called Daughters of Saint Anne, since in her family caring for the sick was taken on as a fourth vow. Sviscerate, in M. Rosa's language, means without a heart of charity.

5 A fine conclusion, calling them to encourage one another in so holy and noble a service and to commit themselves personally and as a community. She awaits their promise in a letter ablaze with charity, to be a consolation to her.

6 For her part she can wish them nothing more sublime: to grow in the way of charity until you are consumed.

She approves the decisions taken about some Sisters. As for what she says about the Parish Priest, she is not to worry but stay at peace; our work must be only to please good God. In Rome all is going fairly well. The Superior of Nizza needs a cook Sister; she is to send her one. The Mother has accepted two postulants and will bring them to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I am answering yours at once, having just finished reading it. As for the teacher, what you thought of doing is fine; don't send her away now, but do as you say in your letter.

  2. I hear about Sr. A. Augusta and am sorry; be patient; make her understand that when you speak with that person you need to be alone, meaning that these are entirely confidential matters; but she must be well persuaded about everything you do, since you are the Superior.2

  3. I hear about the Parish Priest, and about the Morte too. How dreadful! Arm yourself with patience and try to do everything peacefully, without getting upset at all. All will go well if you act calmly. Let them say and do what they like; remember that we are poor servants of the Lord and that our work must be to please good God, our Father.3

  4. As for our business, we are right back at the beginning, and worse; may God's will be done in us: that is all I wish for.4

  5. Courage, and take care of yourself, for it pains me when I hear you are unwell; eat meat.

  6. Listen: [through] those who come to Bologna to join Sr. A. del Sacro Cuore, send her her clock, the one you used to have, also some material to make an apron, and a couple of petticoats for Sr. A. Cherubina.5

  7. You tell me nothing about the row you wanted to have, nor anything about that person's journey to Cremona. How I laughed today on hearing about the Marchioness! I had no doubt it would happen; as the proverb says, what goes around comes around.6

  8. I received a letter from the girl Giuditta saying how very sorry she was at the news of my health, and it had no stamp. Who posted it for her? Who gave her the envelope, the sealing wax? See whether she sent it secretly; keep an eye out without their realizing it was I who told you.7

  9. Our little chapel is a real gem; yesterday I received a fine gift of a chalice for Foligno, holy pictures, books; in short, the wardrobe, I mean the chest of drawers, is almost full again.8

  1. Here everything is going fairly well; Carlottina has been at the Parrocchietta since Sunday and is better; I am as usual.

  2. Sr. A. Giuseppa tells me to send her whoever we like, but what she needs most is a cook and a teacher, and she badly needs the cook; I would say don't send her Sr. A. Angelica, but send [another] cook instead; you can clothe her and then send her. That's well thought out; Sr. A. Angelica would go and stir up a revolution; keep her with you, and when I come we'll think about it.9

  3. Here I have accepted two postulants and shall bring them with me; one may come accompanied by a Superior of the Sisters of Charity.

  4. I hope you have found the Sister to send to Foligno and here together with Sacro Cuore. Goodbye. Greet everyone and Sr. A. Augusta; tell her I shall soon send her the letter to copy; and you look for a nice prize and then send it directly; I'll send you the address.10

Goodbye. [Your most affectionate Mother Rosa]

1 The date is inferred from the context.

Sr. A. Augusta Biagini had taken offence because Sr. A. Francesca, having Institute matters to discuss with Fr Tornatore, had not let her be present. The Mother advises persuading her by explaining the reason.

3 The Parish Priest Elia Magnani was interfering improperly in the running of the school, dealing with the school authorities as if the school depended on him. So says Francesca in an undated letter, presumably related to what the Mother states.

4 About the Rules, which had not yet been revised. This became for her an exercise in abandonment to God's will.

5 Cf. L 101,2. A couple of petticoats for Sr. A. Cherubina Bartoli.

6 That person, Fr Tornatore. There is no information to understand better what had happened. Marchioness Fanny Anguissola Visconti di Mondrone.

7 Giuditta Ruschioni, who entered in 1868. The Mother warns her because she wants to prevent subterfuge and lack of trust in the Superior among the girls.

8 It is not known which little chapel she means; there were by now four houses in Rome.

10 Cf. L 99,4. The letter to be copied is the one to accompany the gift to be sent to Mgr Negrotto (cf. L 101,4).

She tells her about two Sisters' departure and asks whether and how many reduced-fare tickets she has received from Florence. For the Sisters who need sea bathing, she should write to Don Accinelli. A postulant will arrive.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Two lines in haste to tell you that Sr. A. Paolina is to stay in Foligno — I'm afraid I didn't write it — and Sr. A. Lucia and Sr. A. del Sacro Cuore are to come to Rome.1

  2. Have you received the tickets from Florence? Write and tell me how many they sent, because we wrote asking them kindly to send you a few more. If they did, we need to know so as to thank him.

  3. Before sending the two Sisters for the baths, it would be good to write to Don Accinelli along these lines: that there are these Sisters greatly in need of the baths and you await a line from him saying whether you may send them or not, if there is room. In fact you can do it at once.2

  4. What about the lottery? When you were here it seemed it was about to be wound up; what are they doing now?3

  5. A postulant I have accepted will reach you from Fiorentino. She will have 200 F. and cloth in addition to her outfit, with pillowcases etc.4

  6. Pay the Parish Priest's two bills. How well this house has turned out for us! If you think fit to send away more girls, do so prudently.5 Give my regards to Sr. A. Augusta, and believe me your

affectionate Mother

1 Sr. A. Paolina Viani (cf. L 100,6) instead of Sr. A. Giacinta, as Don Antonio Accinelli had advised.

2 It was right not only to inform him beforehand but to ask his opinion, given his administrative role in the Genoa house. Cf. L 2, n. 4.

3 The lottery. It had been running for some time, but not all the tickets had been sold.

4 From Fiorentino: Natalina Persiani entered on 5 July. Cf. Reg. Post. 180.

5 With the Parish Priest Don Elia Magnani, for the house in Via della Morte. How well this house has turned out for us. It is not known which house is meant. She advises sending away those girls who had at least one parent or someone able to ensure them an honest and decent life. Cf. L 90,5.

She hopes to be in Ferrara for much of June. She is to have the Sisters and girls pray for two graces: one for Carlotta, the other for the Work.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. A line in my own hand to tell you: try to grant this torment of yours, Signora C., whatever she wants, everything; I understand she is a first-class nuisance, and I sympathize, but patience is needed.1

  2. I hope to be with you all through June; pray, and have your little girls pray for a grace I need so much; if they obtain it for me, I assure you I'll give them a lovely present; and it is — in complete confidence — Carlottina is under treatment and seems already to be beginning to hear in one ear. Ah! my dear daughter, if only the Sacred Heart would give those medicines the power to cure her! What do you think? Have your little angels pray to obtain it for me, and I'll give them a lovely present; they certainly won't expect it.2

  3. The other, which I need, concerns the Work; but that one later.3 For the rest, all you have done is fine, and may the Lord give you his holy blessing. Let us hope all continues well.

Goodbye. Greet the Sisters for me, and believe me your affectionate Mother Rosa

1 ...torment, Signora C. This is Signora Colomba Grampini: cf. L 47, n. 2. Of odd character, she was demanding and a burden on the community (cf. L Bucciotti to M. Rosa, 17 June 1873); cf. L 94,4.5.6.

2 All the anxieties of this mother, sorely tried by her daughter's disability over long years, now converge in the hope of her cure. Carlotta, an attractive young woman, faced life with a firm will to be freed of her affliction and patiently underwent long, tedious treatment, dreaming of the day she would be normal like the others.

3 The other grace concerned the Rules, not yet approved.

She apologizes for an offensive word that slipped out. She suggests how to deal with a Sister who has left the Institute and with the father of a resident girl. She forbids her to do night watches.

A.M.F.

My Franceschina,

1. Listen, don't take amiss the goose in the telegram, because I said it in jest and whoever sent it thought I meant it. Be patient; it is all the effect of my sacrilegious tongue, which so often speaks before the mind has weighed things.1

2. Today the Sisters arrived safely and gave me your letters, to which I reply at once in my own hand on everything you ask.2

  1. First: as for that insolent Prassede, tell her I intend to be reimbursed for all I spent on her for clothing, keep and medicines. Those were the terms we agreed, and if she should dare (dire) say anything, let them consider that I am now tired of it and shall do what must be done; and that she was not sent away but left of her own free will, for we never send away any sick Sister, etc.; I shall come myself.3

  2. Now listen, I give you an obedience, and it is absolute: I don't want you to do night watches at all; not at all, do you understand? The answers you gave Count Cigala are all fine.4

  3. Second: about Albarelli, tell her father that we are not accustomed to sending girls out and then taking them back, not even for bathing. If they go home, it means that once she has left,

tell him you are warning him that she will not be readmitted, and indeed he had better take the other one too. It would have been better if he had paid something and sent her to the nuns, where the others go for their bathing; so if she goes, I don't want her taken back.5

6. Let the whole world talk, and let us do God's will. Forward; I am yours, in haste.

Affectionate Mother Rosa. Tell Sr. A. Augusta I shall write to her tomorrow; yours for ever.6

2 The Sisters... cf. L 100,6; 104,6.

4 Count Domenico Cigala, canon. He took an interest in and helped the girl Anna Ghizzoni, aged 11, who entered the Institute in November 1873.

5 The father, Mr Roberto, lived in Genoa; of his two daughters, Margherita, 16, had entered in October 1869, and Silene, 11, in December 1870.

6 Sr. A. Augusta: cf. L 97, n. 4.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Today I received your letter; I reply at once; as for the Confirmation girls, you did well not to let them receive it; say what you think best, as long as they don't receive it.

  2. Another thing: accept postulants but clothe none; I'll tell you everything when I arrive; at last we have the Rules and can observe them; I shall bring them to you.2

  3. I don't know if you'll understand me, because my head aches and I can't write; I shall not leave Rome until Saturday of next week; plan your letters accordingly: I shall leave on the 21st of this month and stay 8 or 10 days [in Foligno]. I'll stop, having nothing more to tell you. I am your

Affectionate Mother

4. I hope that, with a good number of girls going for the bathing, less will be spent and you can economize a little, and if God sends some money, pay off a few small debts.3 I am glad you can make those oak buttons.4 Meanwhile that's money for the odd expenses.

Sr. A. Augusta's sister will come to Piacenza; she is to prepare a place for her to sleep. The Mother will be in Piacenza by 27 July. There will be no solemn feast for Saint Anne; if the Bishop wishes to come, let it be privately.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. My headache is so bad I can hardly see; yesterday I received yours; now I am letting you know that Sr. A. Augusta's sister will come and will sleep with Sr. A. Vincenza in the room that was fixed up, which was Sr. A. Adelaide's; but on Sr. A. Vincenza's bed I would like you to put the iron frames with the curtain round them, so that no one is disturbed.2

  2. I shall be in Piacenza by 27 July. There will be no feast. A few extra Masses, but all in perfect silence, as if we did not exist.3

  3. If Monsignor wants to come, let it be as in private; say that since the mother is absent and there are so many troubles and little providence, it is being left out and nothing is being done.4

  4. I am very pleased about the linen, of which you say you have so much. Let us bless the Lord for it, who little by little furnishes all his houses.5 Let us hope the means will also come to pay your bills.6

Goodbye. Greet Sr. A. Augusta, and your rece7

Rosa

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 received yours: dated 23 June; Sr. A. Augusta's sister: Anna Biagini; which was Sr. A. Adelaide's (cf. L 60,5). The frames: an iron framework to hold the curtain round the bed, so that Sr. A. Vincenza will feel more private.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us

My daughter,

  1. You will receive this letter from the man. Mgr Negrotto asked me to write and tell you to go to Marchioness Antici in his name and tell her that Mgr Negrotto would like her to come here on Monday at 4, where he too would be, to arrange about the benches.2

1 The date is inferred from the context.

She reports on what she did for God's Work on the journey from Rome to Piacenza. She visited the houses of Foligno and Ferrara and delivered the Rules. In Florence she agreed to open a house, and in Bologna two others. The Piacenza house has grown in numbers, but the means of subsistence have diminished.

Most Rev.d Father

  1. I would have liked to write to you as soon as I reached Piacenza and report on what I did on the journey for God's Work, but my breathlessness prevented me, and only now is it beginning to ease; only an exhaustion of strength remains; I still cannot stay on my feet, and this skeleton collapses on every [side].1 God's will be done.

  2. My Father, how many blessings the poor Daughters of Saint Anne invoke on you every day for the great good you have done us!2

  3. Now I'll tell you everything. I spent 8 days in Foligno and found that little community very well, and on giving them the Rules they began to bless the one who sent them.3 In Florence I arranged to accept a house to be opened in August.4 In Bologna I spent two days at the home of Princ.ss Pallavicini and accepted two more houses: one a small hospital and the other a boarding school for boys of good family.5

  4. In Ferrara I found everything in order, and an observance and peace among those Religious that was moving. The day schools have 212 girls, and the boarders too are well on their way, everything done with the greatest propriety. I gathered them and gave them the copy of the Rules, and with one voice they all blessed their benefactor for having

sent them, and promised to pray that God may fill him with graces.

5. Finally Piacenza, where I found half a village: girls, postulants, religious, all in order and at peace, with exact observance.

  1. Only the means are no longer what they were. My God! You had given me someone who provided them, and you have taken him from me. Your divine Will be done!6

  2. My Father, I found a point in the Rules about Holy Co™ that I do not quite understand. If you will allow me another time to ask you for an explanation, I shall be most grateful.7 Forgive me if I have gone on too long, and meanwhile please bless me, while I remain Your Reverence's Humble Obl. Servant

Sr. A. M. Rosa Gattorno

1 as soon as I reached: she arrived there on the evening of 5 July. Cf. L 117, 1.

2 He had accepted the task, entrusted by the S. Congregation of BB. and RR., of revising the FSA Rule.

3 It may be supposed that in one of their meetings in Rome he had personally allowed the Mother to have the Rules read in the communities.

4 There is no information on this in the letters of this publication.

5 In Bologna, the guest as before of Countess Maria Anna Trotti, Princess Pallavicini; two houses: at Pennabilli, cf. L 127.

6 You had given me someone: Fr Tornatore. Cf. L 68, 5-6.

7 About Holy Communion. Replying on 15 July, he said he would gladly answer her on the point of Communion. And he did, after receiving the requested explanation, on 11 August 1873: «the Holy See does not approve daily Communion in any Constitutions of Sisters, but at most permits it three times... (AFSA, RdP - 30-31, 72).

She warns her to avoid worldly talk when she spends time conversing with the young ladies who come to visit her. She urges her to pray and to love the Lord.

  1. Today, my Eletta, you will allow me to say a little something about the visits you continually receive from the young ladies of Tor de' Specchi.1 I say this not to admonish you, but only as your Mother, who loves you so much and holds you in the Heart of Jesus so as to have you one day beside her in the glory of Heaven, where there are no more troubles or anxieties, but only joy reigns.2

  2. I would like your conversation, when those girls come, always to be edifying — as I am sure it will be; I repeat, you must take these words as thoughts of mine in-sursimi, and you must allow them to me, because I am your Mother, and you know mothers always see things large where their children are concerned: they may see them as saints, yet they are never satisfied with their holiness; such is your Mother; the reason is that everything you say will be noted and they will draw conclusions from it.3

  3. So take care that all your words are edifying, and never answer the slightest question that smacks of earthly things; we must concern ourselves only with God, my Eletta; let us leave the rest to worldly people.4

  4. If you knew what happened to a Superior who thoughtlessly let herself slip into certain conversations about dress. My God! You can imagine what came of it. But enough: I see I am losing myself writing things that are useless for you.5

  5. Let us turn, my daughter, to our own little matters: let us ask

dear Jesus to keep us in his love. Yes, my God, I want my Eletta to be consumed in your side.6

  1. Pray, my dear, for from prayer we have everything; it is there that everything is obtained. Oh, inexhaustible fountain of grace; come, my Eletta, let us draw from this fountain the water of salvation and life.7

  2. You wanted some news about the house of the Morte.8 But what can I do? I am weighed down with work and cannot stop any longer. All yours,

most affectionate Mother Rosa

1 The young ladies of Tor de' Specchi, daughters of the Ladies of the Circle of St Monica, who had come to know her, liked to visit her.

2 Knowing her temperament, she forestalls her: she does not want to admonish her, but as her Mother she wants to guide her, holding her close in the Heart of Jesus, along her own path, whose only goal is the glory of heaven.

3 I would like... your conversation to be always edifying. The expression has a Pauline ring (1 Cor 8:1; 10:23; 14:17). It should be formative, based on matters of vital and moral growth and not on the trivia of a worldly mentality that loves frivolity. This is the central point to be corrected. She puts it with exquisitely motherly tact and pedagogical skill, so that it hits the mark without irritating or wounding and is accepted.

4 She repeats more pointedly: edifying, raising it to a clearly Christian and religious level: God alone! The rest must have no hold on us.

5 To complete the correction, a warning: be careful! It happened to someone else!

6 Here is the remedy: let us ask Jesus to keep us in his love. And she asks it forcefully: Yes, my God, I want my Eletta to be consumed in your side.

7 The conclusion becomes an urgent invitation: pray... let us draw from this fountain the water of salvation and life. It is a proposal and a promise of a communion of souls in Jesus, the one fountain.

8 Compared with what she has said, the news Eletta wants does not seem so important, and she cuts it short; this too is part of her pedagogy. The letter had its effect. Sr. A. Eletta replied on 14 July: «...how your words touch my heart... I truly promise to follow your motherly and wise advice». AFSA, F35.

She did not reply sooner because of her health. She asks whether she is returning to Genoa, though she wishes to stay in Rome, land of the Saints, where everything helps on the way of holiness.

My Emilia,

  1. If I have not answered your letter until now, you will know from the Superior that the breathlessness I had in Rome has kept me company and indeed has not yet left me; but I am much better; the baths, the air, everything seems to help me.1

  2. And you, my dear, what are you doing? Are you thinking of leaving the holy city and coming, or rather going, home?2 You are right to like it there; in the land of the saints everything breathes the perfume of heavenly holiness and greatly helps one to advance on the way of perfection — you who desire nothing but to become a saint.3

  3. May God grant it, for I wish it for you with all my soul, there being no other good but this. In haste, your very poor

Friend Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 Cf. L 114,1; 117,1.

2 Emilia's visit to Rome is mentioned in the correspondence between M. Rosa and Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino. Cf. L 109, n. 1. going home? returning to Genoa.

3 Emilia did not enter religious life, unlike her sister Anna, who did in 1874.

She is rather unwell and very weak. Sr. A. Vincenza has left, so she is alone in dealing with the correspondence. That is why she will not be able to write to him often.

A.M.F.

My good Father Agostino,

  1. This time the weakness will not leave me; the breathlessness has lessened, but my strength is completely gone; I cannot stand at all, especially today.1

  2. Yesterday I received your letter with news of the Superior; how grieved I was! God's will be done in all things!2

  3. You will have received one from Sr. A. Vincenza, who left for Genoa at 4 this morning with Carlottina; so imagine, I am alone at the desk while the correspondence grows every day, and writing costs me a great deal. So if you see that I write little, think who is preventing me.

  4. Send me the Sacred Hearts;3 send one to Foligno; and believe me, as I feel I can go on no longer, yours for ever

Sr. Anna M. Rosa Gattorno

1 She had begun to feel ill even before leaving Rome.

2 On 12 July he had given her precise details of Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi's illness, though she was already better and without fever.

3 Fr Agostino had a nephew of his paint the pictures the Mother wanted (Sacred Heart of Jesus, Saint Anne) for each Chapel of the Institute. Cf. L 27, n. 2.

Various news and advice about the house. She has sent the regulations and will soon write to the Canon.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just one line to tell you that yesterday I received your last letter, telling me about the Superior's health and Don Giovanni; you did well to answer as you did about the nun: she must never join you in any common act, only at prayers, but not at the examen. You did well.2

  2. Show this excellent Canon — who I tell you is an angel for us — all the needs of the house and commend yourself to him; you will have everything.

  3. I sent at once the regulations that had stayed among my papers; copy them, so that one copy stays with you and the other with the Ladies;3 I shall soon write to the Canon, but you should know that I am alone at the desk, Sr. A. Vincenza having left for Genoa, and I am unwell.4

  4. Make sure the religious do not confide in this former religious at all, and that the girls behave well.

I am your affectionate Mother

5. God bless you together with the whole community. I hope you will have realized the mistake I made in sending you the [letter]; for charity's sake keep it and show it to no one. Yesterday I received your letter; you did everything well. You will see that the Canon will see to the rest and to all you need.

Goodbye.

1 The addressee's name is missing in the original, but it is clear from Cocchella's letter (11 July '73) to which the Mother is replying.

2 The health of Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi, Superior at Tor de' Specchi; Don Giovanni means Rinaldo De Giovanni, who was involved in the work as Director and had asked her about Carolina

Giorgi, a former Dominican staying there; not at the examen, that is, at the evening prayer during which the Sisters made their examination of conscience on the day.

3 The Regulations, composed by M. Rosa, had been taken away by her inadvertently. The other copy to the Ladies of the «Pious Union of Lady Protectors of Women in Service».

4 Cf. L 117,3.

She is pleased with the news from Genoa, except about Alessandro. She may go to visit her sister, but making sure Carlotta is well looked after and Anna stays with the religious. She expects her on the 26th.

A.M.F.

My be[loved] daughter,

  1. Yesterday I wrote you a note and today another, just as yesterday I received one from you and today another. I am glad to hear so much good news from Genoa and everyone. Only about Alessandro am I anxious, because Carlotta tells me he is ill. My God! what suffering!1

  2. Vincenza, you ask whether you may go to your sister; yes, go at once, at once; see whether you can leave Carlotta in Sr. A. del Buon Pastore's care together with Anna.2

  3. Make sure you leave Anna and Carlotta in Albaro, but Anna is never to go there when you are not there; she must always stay with the nuns; tell Carlotta so, for pity's sake.3

  4. Then I think you could come on Saturday, after the ceremony, with the Genoese postulant who entered recently. If Santi has this postulant's money, get it from him and bring it to me.4

  5. Then you can leave on the5 afternoon one; I need you to come as soon as you can.

  6. For pity's sake don't overdo it; take care of your health. If you love me as you say, you must keep well and look after yourself. For charity's sake see that it comes back; I am extremely anxious. Write at once that (è ar)you are taking the pills again.

7. My liver trouble seems to be getting worse; writing is an effort; I need you back on Saturday evening. I expect you, of course, on the 26th. I can hardly believe it will be done that day.6

Goodbye. Yours for all ages, amen.

[Mother Rosa]

1 Carlotta had written on the 16th: «Uncle Federico told me: sorrow because my Gigino is ill».

2 She had asked to visit her sister Emilia, who was ill. Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore Dosi was in Genoa for sea bathing, as was Anna Biagini. Cf. L 112,4.

3 The Mother's precautionary measures.

4 Saturday 26th, feast of Saint Anne, after the clothing ceremony of the two postulants in the Sampierdarena house. The postulant's details are missing. Father Santi, cf. L 11, n. 3.

5 The afternoon train.

6 She awaits that day eagerly.

She has decided to send the Superior Francesca to stay a few days with Carlotta. She should ask Sr. A. Santina to put them both up. She is not to tire herself. She is to bring the postulant's money.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. As for the money you mention having handed over to you — that is, the small savings made — no; but if some comes in, then bring it to me.2

  2. As for Carlotta, I thought of sending the Superior Francesca on Monday morning; for Sunday, ask Sr. A. Santina to keep them both there in Genoa; meanwhile I hear there is a ceremony. Francesca will come on Monday.3

  3. Please don't tire yourself, for pity's sake; I am anxious, you cannot imagine. Bring the postulant's two hundred francs.4

Goodbye, for I am in a hurry; yours (tu) for ev[er].

[Mother Rosa]

1 The date is inferred from the letter of 18.7 she is answering.

2 Money. Sr. A. Vincenza had asked whether she should bring to Piacenza the 150 francs saved by the Sampierdarena house.

3 Sr. A. Santina Solenghi, Superior of the Genoa house, was to keep Carlotta and Anna Biagini with her until the Superior Francesca Camisa arrived from Piacenza. I hear there is a ceremony: the Archbishop was to come for the clothing.

4 The details of the postulant accepted in the Sampierdarena house are missing.

She gives her some errands and urges her to put the community in order and identify a Sister who could be Superior.

A.M.F.

My daughter D...

  1. So I write to you every day. Look, my dear, today first I'll tell you I need you to send me the pills for the Superior Francesca at once, because she is not very well. Then tell Don Accinelli to write two lines to Don Giovanni, who would like them.2

  2. I hear all you tell me about this poor house; I weep over it. For pity's sake, my Vincenza, try to set things in order, but don't overwork. Woe to you if you disobey in this. Give orders, but don't do the work.3

  3. Please see whether there is anyone who could serve as superior.4 Vincenza, I tell you, I command you to look after yourself, for charity's sake. I am tired of seeing the sick and the dead. Do you understand me? Goodbye, I am yours for all ages,

affectionate Mother Rosa

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Vincenza's reply of 20 July.

2 Don Giovanni Biale: cf. L 142,5.

3 This is the Sampierdarena house, where Sr. A. Vincenza had to restore order both in observance and in the running of the boarding school.

4 Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi was too kind; a stronger, more decisive Superior was needed, but Sr. A. Vincenza saw no one suitable.

She is to go on holiday with Sr. A. Panasia, informing the Superintendent and the Countess beforehand. She should tell the other Sisters that they too will have a period of rest. She is to leave the house in good order and come to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Yesterday I received your letter and reply at once, first blessing God for inspiring those good gentlemen.1

  2. As for Sr. A. Panasia, you can take her away with you at once; first inform the Superintendent, telling him she needs her native air during these two months of holiday. Write the same to the Countess: that you have arranged everything with the Superintendent, who is content provided she is there for the school year.2

  3. And (le) tell the Countess that you too have 5 days' holiday and are coming to see everyone, then returning to your post, and that on your return, when you are alone, you will visit her. Do you understand me?3

  4. Let Sr. A. Beatrice and Maddalena stay with the girls, and Sr. A. Cecilia keep an eye on them all day;4 if these two do well, tell them that on your return you will give them too a few days of recreation, which I shall see to. Hold St. A. on Sunday, as you say; do as you think best.5

  5. I warn you that on Tuesday of next week, the 29th of this month, I leave, so if you come on Monday I shall still see you and we shall talk and arrange everything; in person we shall organize it better. I hope you will understand this letter, though written in haste. Goodbye, your

affectionate Mother

1 The Superintendent and the Inspector, who declined the invitation to attend the girls' examinations.

2 Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi, the teacher, was temperamental; her behaviour and lack of serious, steady commitment harmed the school. Cf. Bucciotti Letters, AFSA, F30.

3 Countess Maria Anna Trotti; do you understand me? She was not to tell her of Sr. A. Panasia's transfer.

4 She explains how to share out the tasks during her absence: Sr. A. Beatrice Merici with the postulant Maddalena Carmeli; Sr. A. Cecilia Tortini was to oversee the general running.

She orders her not to tire herself, to take care of herself and be serene, for she is close to her; and on behalf of Marchioness Carrega she asks her to collect some items.

Dear Vincenza,

  1. I command you not to overwork, because it distresses me greatly; I want you to take warm goat's milk in the morning. For charity's sake don't distress me further by being unwell. Be of good heart, for I am always close to you.2

  2. Marchioness Carrega tells me Signora Baiardo owes her some items; have (te) them handed to you, and she will come and collect them. I'll close, for I am worried about Carlotta. Goodbye, my daughter, I am yours for an eternity. Greetings to Ninetta.3

[Affectionate Mother Rosa]

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 She encourages her. One notes her solicitude and anxiety for Sr. A. Vincenza, whose health was rather delicate.

3 Marchioness Carrega: she does not specify whether Emilia, Anna or the mother. Signora Baiardo was an acquaintance of the Rapallino family. Ninetta: Anna Biagini, then in Genoa.

4 Whether Sr. A. Panasia is well. In the same letter of 22 July the Superior had told her: “Sr. A. Panasia is a lamb, without my having to correct her”.

She has sent her a parcel, sorry not to have been able to include a small present for the Countess. She is to leave on Sunday, telling the Countess that on her return she will stop with her in Bologna.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have sent the parcel with books and little pictures, pillowcases and a shawl for Signora Colomba;l I could not send you the item for the Countess, to my great regret, though I did all I could to send it. But what can you do? We are in Piacenza, and that's that!2

  2. For the rest, you can quite well leave on Sunday afternoon on the last train, which arrives here at 10.3 I shall send for you when I have a telegram. I think it leaves Ferrara at 5 p.m. Goodbye; I add no more because I am unwell and alone. God bless you, and believe me

[your most affectionate Mother Rosa]

3. I think I wrote to you to let the Countess know of your departure, telling her you will call on your way back, when you will be alone or with someone you can leave at the station. If Sr. A. Panasia is well and you see she can do well and is truly converted, then leave her, giving her very strict orders so that no trouble arises.4

1 The Superior had asked for little gifts as prizes for the girls and a present for the Countess's name day. Signora Colomba Grampini was in the Ferrara house. Cf. L 94,4; 106, n. 1.

2 Piacenza is the house of poverty.

3 On 27 July. The Mother was to leave on the 29th, so she could confer with her at leisure. Cf. L 123,5.

4 If Sr. A. Panasia is well. In the same letter of 22 July the Superior had told her: Sr. A. Panasia is a lamb, without my having to correct her.

She refuses some requests. She deplores the irresponsible behaviour of some nursing Sisters and admonishes them to mend their ways.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. In this letter of yours, just received, you ask to visit the nuns: I answer absolutely not; you ask whether you may go to make novenas and so on in churches not our own: I repeat, no;2 you tell me the nurses are in demand, lose more than one night's sleep and do everything willingly. I tell you that the day before yesterday I had a letter that stabbed my soul, from what this noble Lady told me about the nurses when they cared for Marchioness Costaguti.3

  2. They did not give her the medicine the doctor had prescribed on time; they took fright when she was delirious and went to call the people of the house. Finally they left the patient for hours on the pretext of going to lunch. How dreadful! when you know well that one must take turns and never leave such patients; in short, she told me so many things, and so did a Priest, my God!4

  3. Tell these wretches that they are the disgrace of the House and of the whole Institute. Alas, they have pierced my soul!5

  4. Have the Superior of Tor de' Specchi read these two lines concerning the nurses, for I cannot write so much, being very ill and without Sr. A. Vincenza.6 Goodbye, my daughter; encourage these scatterbrains; tell them the hon-

our of the Institute depends on them, and that I thought I had called nurses whom I was told were good; a delusion — quite the opposite.7 God bless you, and everyone. I am your affectionate

M. R.

1 The date is inferred from the letter she is answering, dated 20 July 1873.

2 The Sister wanted to visit the «Brignole Nuns» of the Hospice of S. Maria degli Angeli, where some of her old school companions were, to ask them for something for the house.

3 She had written verbatim: the Sisters «strive to observe our holy Rules and are always generous; since we have many sick, although they work by day, some for the sick, some at the laundry, yet when I give the obedience they all offer themselves with great fervour; often, to my regret, I give in, and so they lose two nights in a row, although the Superior of Tor de' Specchi lends me some of hers. They lose two nights in a row: they lose sleep...

4 .…did not give her the medicine... the reports M. Rosa had received from other sources (Marchioness Costaguti and a Priest) differed, however, from the Superior's. A Priest was Costaguti's confessor, a certain Fr Agostino, as Sr. A. Eletta Bruschi wrote to M. Rosa on 28 July 1873.

5 wretches, because they gave a bad image of the Institute.

6 Sr. A. Vincenza was in Genoa.

7 She had herself looked for and asked the Superiors for «good nurses».

She explains how to arrange the relief of the nursing Sisters caring for the sick at home and what food they should receive there.

Read this letter to all the Sisters.

A.M.F.

The blessing of the Eternal Father be with us all

My daughter,

Blessed be our Mother Saint Anne, Mother of the Immaculate

  1. You ask about the sick outside the City; listen: they should go, for instance, this evening and stay all night and the next day, and then the others go to relieve them;2 they take the omnibus, because they may separate only in Convents; there they can stay from two to 6 days, because one sleeps while the other watches;3 but in private houses this is not allowed: you must change every 24 hours.

  2. As for food: in the morning milk and coffee; at midday soup, two dishes and a piece of fruit; in the evening just one thing; I think I have made myself clear.

  3. For charity's sake let them never separate, because if they had to stay longer you see they would have to separate; be careful, for pity's sake.4

  4. I hear you are happy. Now another thing: listen, this time you allowed the Sisters to take cof-

fee with Defilippi, and since he was with Don Accinelli there is no harm, but with anyone, never again; make it clear it is not to be done again.5 Goodbye, dear daughter. I am your

[affectionate Mother Rosa]

2 It is clear: with lay people the Sisters must always be in pairs and may stay the night and the following day. They are to travel by omnibus.

3 In convents, however, two Sisters may stay up to six consecutive days.

4 because... separate. She means: they must never separate, and if they have to stay longer and you see that it is necessary for them to separate, let it be treated as an exceptional case requiring the greatest care.

5 Defilippi, of the Priests of the Mission, confessor of the two Piacenza communities, had visited Genoa.

  1. A line in haste; I have received your letter. Listen, now I want you, my daughter, to send me Sr. A. Giovannina with the postulant here to Nizza, where I am, so that she may get better and recover; it would be a pity to lose her.1

She should be cheerful, for she will soon receive the religious habit. She is to pray and look after herself so as to become strong and serve God alone, and prepare for her clothing by detaching herself from everything to live for God alone.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line to tell you to be cheerful, for you will soon receive the holy Habit2 and then be transferred and placed somewhere very suitable for you; but a little patience is needed, and with it everything is obtained, together with prayer, for without prayer we are barren trees and can give nothing good. Our fruits — if we bear any — will always be unripe.3
