  1. Please be so kind as to get these two lines to Sister Sr. A. Angela in complete secrecy.2

  2. Now I urge that in your house no religious take the liberty of addressing another familiarly.3 My good Superior, for charity's sake, be watchful; I confess that perhaps this bad habit crept in because I gave a bad example, but from now on it will not happen again, and I ask pardon of God and of them for the bad example.4

  3. Thank you ever so much for the decoction you sent me with the sweet bread.5

  4. I would like to know whether you received my letter, with Sr. A. Vincenza's telling you about Alessandro. I am also writing now to Don Accinelli; he will tell you why.6 In haste, I am your

affectionate Mother

5. Have prayers said; commend me to the Sisters, ask them to pray and make a novena for me to the Sacred Heart of Mary of desperate causes, which has its own prayer; I need a grace, and I hope they will make it fervently.7 God bless you all, you and the alms-collectors in particular.

1 Assumed to be later than L 132, given the reference to the decoction she had received and not yet thanked her for.

2 Sr. A. Angela Degrossi, in Sampierdarena. It was a confidential letter.

3 Addressing familiarly («tu»). The Rules prescribed the formal «lei» between Sisters.

4 She blames herself for the habit that had crept in, though she was not obliged to observe that rule.

5 The decoction, prepared by Signora Maddalena Bacigalupo of Genoa, was effective.

6 Don Accinelli. Cf. L 2, n. 4.

7 The grace of winning the lawsuit brought by Don Angelo Ricchini. Cf. L 84, n. 2.

She asks for his kind intervention to obtain Father Tornatore's readmission to the Institute.

My most Reverend Father,

  1. I take this opportunity to tell you some confidential things I would not dare to send by post.

  2. Do you, my Father, want me obedient? I promise to be so; by God's grace I hope to keep this treasure until death; Most Reverend Father, since I cannot go into detail about my situation, I shall ask my Eletta to do so.1 If good God gives me life and what I need, I shall soon be at your feet and tell you better in person.

  3. Meanwhile, knowing how great your charity is towards the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, I make bold to ask, for the good of this Institute, a grace that is in your hands to grant: in short, the reinstatement of Mr Tornatore.2

  4. Oh! how much toil it would spare me, and how much more peacefully I could come and enjoy the blessed air of this Land of the Saints; but how?3 Most Reverend Father, to the many proofs of protection you have already given this work of the Lord add this one, and I promise that if I have a place in Paradise I shall never cease praying for Your Most Reverend Paternity, as I poorly do now.

  5. I await the longed-for answer anxiously; the Holy Father can do everything.

  6. Thank you for the care you take of those Daughters of Saint Anne.4 Forgive the poor handwriting, but my skeleton can do no better, being very weak.

She encourages her to go forward in a spirit of sacrifice and for love of the Lord. She answers her questions about the work and tells her not to go to the sick; she is to stop nursing when the Schools begin.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. As soon as I arrived last night from Ferrara, where I had been called by Countess Trotti, I read your letters1, which were no small consolation.

2. My daughter, courage! Good God is greatly pleased with sacrifices. Ah! Yes! for his work one must give without stint.

So then, he gave all his blood for us, and we must do the same; yes! blood for blood! Isn't that so, my daughter?2

3. Now to what you ask: to the President, regarding the girls, that's fine; regarding the confessor, always answer that you depend only (que) on the Mother and can neither add nor remove anything without her orders.3

4. As for taking that girl who you say also has a sister who is a teacher, you do well not to take her.4

5. Don't go to the sick yourself, because you will (te) wear yourself out,5 and once you have started school none of you is to go any more, because I don't want those who teach to do nursing. If they want nurses they will call others, and then I'll send you two more, who will do the nursing. You, I don't want.

6. Take care of yourself. I hear poultry is cheap, and meat too; you'd better eat that rather than polenta,6 because I fear it may disagree with you; so try to eat meat, which is the best and healthiest food.

Goodbye, it is late; the Lord bless you with the others, and believe me always

your affectionate MOTHER ROSA GATTORNO

1 The Sister had written her three letters with precise reports on all that was happening in the house, opened only a few days before; the Sisters had in fact arrived in Pennabilli on 10 October '73. Cf. L 127, 128, 129 and Appendix IV.

2 One must give without stint. The place, in the province of Pesaro, 76 km from the provincial capital and 550 m above sea level, seemed to the Sisters going there for the first time "on top of such a high mountain" and out of the world; after 5 hours by carriage from Rimini, "seeing the village, our melancholy grew". So wrote Sr. A.

Francesca Camisa, who with Don Accinelli had accompanied the four Sisters. (Cf. L Camisa: 9.10.1873). And Sr. A. Carlotta on 13.10, after Francesca's departure: "you cannot believe what anguish weighs on my heart, how sensitive I feel at finding myself in this place; I seem to have no more hope of seeing anyone again". The Mother sets before her the supernatural motives and the one Model: Jesus. He gave everything for us... yes, blood for blood. And she awaits, before him, her assent: Isn't that so, my daughter? concentrating in that final phrase, together with the love of God, her mother's love.

3 The President, Luigi Piccini, had asked whether they forbid the girls "to go to worldly amusements, such as the theatre, etc.". She had replied that this is the parents' responsibility (L 15.10.73). The confessor had asked whether they went to the parish for Mass (ibid.).

4 The same Sister, in passing on the request, had expressed a contrary opinion.

5 The Superior too had gone to nurse the sick. At home, however, there was much to do. I teach the two Sisters, I am a bit of a nurse,

wardrobe keeper, sacristan, but above all cook. We eat a lot of polenta (L 17.10.73).

6 The Mother was very attentive to the Sisters' health.

Dietary advice for the teaching Sister. She may accept the postulant if she thinks fit, and should do all she can to secure the front door of the house properly from inside.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just finished reading your letter and reply at once, enclosing one for the teacher;1 listen, my dear, try to give the teacher coffee every afternoon after lunch, and in the evening broth, a little soup with a bit of meat even on days of abstinence; see whether with tamarind and the like you can stop her diarrhoea; I hope that if she is well looked after she will manage everything.

2. Make the postulant aware of our obligations, then accept her.

3. Listen, as for the oil for the sanctuary lamp, those of the Congregation must supply it; of course you must use what they supply for your own use.2

4. The Superior tells me that a doctor also has a key to your front door and can come in whenever he likes.3 Listen, have a bolt put on the door at once, and tell the President you are frightened when you hear it open; then go to the Bishop in confidence — indeed leave the Sister in the anteroom (for we may be alone with Bishops) — and tell him: "Monsignor, I must tell you something in confidence", and disclose the matter, saying you are afraid and I place everything in Your Excellency's hands, as our Father. This I do by written order of my Mother, who also sends you her respects.4

5. Try to eat meat, which is the healthiest food. My daughter, courage. As for the young girl, accept her if you think fit.5

Goodbye, my dear; the Lord bless you with your Sisters, and believe me your affect.

MOTHER

6. P.S. Tell Sr. A. Adelaide I shall send the shifts together with your things.6

1 The teacher is Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini.

2 The "Congregation of Charity" of Pennabilli.

3 The Superior Francesca Camisa, who had accompanied the Sisters. Cf.

L 135, n. 2.

4 The President of the Congregation of Charity: Luigi Piccini. The Bishop,

Mgr Luigi Mariotti, resided at Pennabilli.

5 Cf. L 135,6. The young girl is the postulant of par. 2.

6 Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini.

She is glad to hear of the welcome they received from the Holy Father and hopes it will spur them on to observe the Rules. Patience in their straits, and forward with courage in her task as Superior.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line for you too. I received your letter with the two little holy pictures.2 I am glad to hear of the consoling welcome you had from the Holy Father.3 I hope it will encourage you (a) more and more to observe your holy Rules, and in particular the chapter about never receiving alone persons of the other sex, neither priests nor lay people, whoever they may be. In short, if you are faithful to this Rule, I assure you the holy Mother will help you and give you courage to observe all the others.

2. I am very sorry to hear of your straits, but patience is needed. Let us hope that when the Ladies return from the country you will have more help.4

3. For charity's sake do all you can to keep these ladies5 happy, and see to cleanliness, I beg you, for it would grieve me greatly to hear complaints about it. Be vigilant; the Superior must be all eyes and always turning like a spinning wheel, so that nothing escapes her. Courage, my dear; let us do all our work for the Lord.6 Goodbye, I am your

affectionate M. ROSA. I don't know if you'll understand, it is so badly written.

1 This letter was catalogued among the undated ones addressed to Sr. A. Vincenza

Rapallino, though dated 24 October 1872. The year, however, is wrong, since at that time the Daughters of Saint Anne had no house in Rome. It must therefore be from 24 October 1873. As for the addressee, since at this time

Rapallino was not in Rome and the content answers a letter of Sr. A. Del

S. Cuore Cocchella written to M. Rosa on 21.10.1873, it must be the latter.

2 The Sister wrote to her: "by good fortune the Holy Father gave me two little holy pictures, and I want to give them to you, my good Mother, as a pledge of the gratitude I bear you for all the care lavished on my well-being, and I ask you to accept my heart in them...".

3 The Holy Father had received the Daughters of Saint Anne on Sunday 19 October.

4 your straits. "Canon De Giovanni (the administrator of the Pious Union) is always distressed by the same trouble, namely that we lack money... Marchioness Cavalletti is still in Frascati", she had written four days earlier.

5 The ladies of the Pious Union for the Protection of servant girls.

6 the Superior must. Being responsible, she must keep track of everything:

the "girls at risk" in residence, to be cared for and educated, prepared for life and found a position, generally in service with good families; the work at home: laundry and ironing for others, to meet the needs of the house; home nursing of the sick, day and night; the good running of the community.

She encourages her in her task as Superior, suggesting how to care for a sick Sister and how to resolve matters in the house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I have just received your letter and hear what you tell me about the teacher Sr. Anna Adelaide. Listen, keep this timetable with her: let her sleep in the morning; at midday try to give her meat, and in the evening a little soup. My dear, patience is needed for this year.2

2. God wants to make martyrs of us thus; his cross must be everywhere, and in this town, for you, it is this. Courage!3

3. Tell the President I hope he will find the Prefect favourable to us. As for the Thursday school, go along with them, since it is only for one hour.4

4. Try to get the President and the Bishop to decide soon to send for two more. Tell the Bishop tactfully, asking him to write to me so that I send two more at once, and the same with the President. With tact you will see you get everything, but always peacefully.5

5. Don't be upset, for charity's sake, about Sr. A. Adelaide; treat her as a sick person. Be patient. I hope you received my second letter enclosing one for Sr. A. Adelaide.6 See that the food is wholesome, with meat; I hear chickens are cheap; you can buy and eat them.7

6. Courage, daughter, for the time of suffering has come! Embrace it gladly and never let it go to waste; remember that this Mother of yours holds you every day in the Heart of Jesus, who wants you all his, and so mine for ever,8 while I remain your

most affectionate MOTHER. God bless you and the community.

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Carlotta's reply of 27 October: "This evening I received yours..." and also from the context.

2 Sr. A. Adelaide's health is delicate. Cf. L 136,1.

3 Here is the concreteness of the cross: in this town, for you, it is this.

4 Regarding the school. The Sisters had been asked to give literacy lessons to adults.

5 Since there were sick people to nurse at home, it was good for the authorities to ask her for two more religious.

6 This is L 136.

7 Cf. L 135,6; 136,5.

8 The Sister replied: "You cannot believe, dear Mother, how glad I was to hear that you hold me every day to the Heart of Jesus, and so I gladly embrace the Cross the Heavenly Spouse gives me".

She thanks him and reports on the Lord's Work: she has accepted requests to open new houses; 15 religious were clothed and there will be another clothing in early November; aspirants are numerous. Good is being done and prayers are said for the Holy Father and for him.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. As soon as my health improved, I would have liked to fulfil my duty of thanking Your Most Reverend Eminence for the great kindness of sending me so salutary a blessing from our Holy Pope Pius IX, and at the same time to report on the Lord's Work and the Houses opened since I left Rome, now seventeen in number, with other requests from various towns such as Acqui, Turin and small villages of the Monferrato.1

2. I can assure you that while I was opening these Houses I was always sorry not to have asked your Apostolic blessing beforehand, and, wanting to ask it in my own hand, I could never find a suitable moment to do so.2

3. Most Reverend Eminence, bless then these Houses and those I must now open. Amid so many adversities some good is still being done, and many prayers rise to God, most of them for the Pope and for Your Most Reverend Eminence, to whom I owe so much.3

4. On St Francis's day fifteen Religious were clothed, and on All Saints' day there will be another four, leaving still a good number of aspirants.

5. If my health, or rather my wretched strength, permits, I had planned to come to

Rome4 on the first of January and at once be at your feet to receive your pastoral blessing, which I await prostrate, remaining with the greatest respect and veneration

Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble Daughter and Servant Sr. ANNA

MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 Since I left. She had left Rome on 21 June. She had opened other houses: at Pennabilli and Cortemaggiore, and had received requests to open in other towns.

2 On other occasions, before starting new works, the Mother had asked for his pastoral blessing as Vicar of the Holy Father. Cf. Lettere 2, L 4 and in this volume L 391.

3 Her love for the Church was most lively and active.

4 She actually went to Rome on 16 January 1874.

The priest of Genoa, whose dispute he knows of, having been condemned in the Court of Cassation, has had her summoned again, so that she must answer with "oaths". She will write to the Bishop of Genoa to prevent this. She asks him to have Cardinal Vannicelli intervene to put an end to the matter.

My most Reverend Father,

1. When one is in difficulty, to whom should one turn but to him who has always been my help and comfort? To you, my good Father. What can I say: tribulations love me faithfully and I embrace them heartily, since they are my only companions on this earth; they are right: they see me alone in the martyrdom of this Work, and so they strive to crush me. God wills it, may his divine will be done; if it is the will of men, one day they will see the result.

2. Today, just as I came out of church, I was handed a thick letter containing a transcribed Summons from that priest of Genoa1 whom Your Most Reverend Eminence kindly took up with the Archbishop;2 but evidently nothing was done about this wretched man, for having completely lost the suit and seen his hopes dashed in the Court of Cassation too, he has had me summoned to swear on oath about things that make one blush with shame that a priest could go so far and that in a Diocese like Genoa he should be allowed to do so unpunished.3

3. I am having it copied for you, so that you may read it and speak of it to our defending Angel, His Most Reverend Eminence,4 and at the same time I have thought of sending a copy to the Archbishop of Genoa himself, asking him to put a stop to such scandal.5

4. If His Most Reverend Eminence would also deign to support it with a recommendation of his own — and he could make it stronger — you can do everything. For pity's sake, don't abandon me at this sad moment.

5. My God! my whole life for your work, but swear an oath, no; I would rather suffer a thousand martyrdoms than do such a thing, I who am horrified by the very word oath.6

6. Write me something, for charity's sake; commend me to His Most Reverend Eminence, for with his protection I hope for everything. Forgive me for continually troubling you, but you know I have no one. One more thing I would ask: should I also send a copy to the Most Rev. Sallua? What do you say?7 I await your reply.

Bless me, and have His Eminence bless me, which I await prostrate, remaining Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Daughter Sr. A. MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 the priest is Angelo Ricchini. Cf. L 84; 91.

2 Cf. L 84, n. 2. Cardinal Vannicelli, having received from Ricchini "a printed pamphlet" against the Foundress, had had the Archbishop of Genoa written to "so that he might try to put a stop to so great a scandal, since it came from a priest subject to him" (L Wanstienkist 4.5.73 to M. Rosa - AFSA, 83).

3 he has had me summoned to swear. On 25 October '73 Don Accinelli had informed her: "Ricchini, as you will see from the enclosed document, which I thought it well to transcribe so that it should not come as a surprise, invites you to swear; so you should prepare written answers to these questions with maturity and reflection" (AFSA,

AA1 73,34).

4 She sends a copy of the oaths to the "defending Angel", Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli, Protector of the Institute.

5 Cf. L 141.

6 It meant appearing in court and swearing the "oaths" demanded by Ricchini. It cost her a great deal.

7 Fr Vincenzo Sallua was a Consultor of the "Holy Office". Cf. L 91.

She has received the summons, which she encloses; she has sent a copy to the Cardinal Protector. She expresses confidence that he will support her in putting an end to the proceedings.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. Yesterday I received from my attorney Don Accinelli in Genoa the enclosed document, which was utterly heartrending merely to read. How can a Priest say so many things, all twisted and false? Had he summoned me to Your Excellency's feet, I would gladly have accepted, and received from those blessed hands with the greatest pleasure any punishment Your Excellency saw fit to give; but to the Civil Courts, my God! what anguish!1

2. Most Reverend Excellency, know that this morning I also sent a copy to our Protector, Cardinal Vannicelli, so that he may tell me what to do, guided by my Superiors, the only support I have to soothe my sorrow...2 just as I am confident of finding in Your Excellency effective support to stop such unseemly proceedings.

Please bless me, Your Excellency, while with the greatest veneration I remain Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Servant Sr. ANNA M. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Cf. L 140.

2 Don Giovanni Bosco had also intervened to settle the dispute between the parties.

Cf. L 84.

She cannot take the girl he recommends into any of the Rome houses, all being very poor; if he wishes, she will take her into the Piacenza house, which she too maintains with great difficulty, having lost the one who helped her. She asks him to obtain a special blessing from the Holy Father for a sick priest.

Most Reverend Monsignor,

1. I have received your esteemed letter and hasten to reply in my own hand. I am very sorry I cannot grant your request, not knowing where to put the girl you recommend, since the Rome houses are very poor and, as Your Excellency knows, are at my expense, the slender allowance they receive not being enough, and Tor de' Specchi is entirely my responsibility.1

2. I would not know where else to send her except Piacenza, where these two years I too have had to struggle to keep it going, having been deprived of my right arm, so that I am alone;2 something I cannot come to terms with, seeing that in these times men who help God's works are so rare, and instead of protecting those who work, they are put in chains.

3. My Monsignor, how many tribulations, persecutions, insults and ill-treatment one swallows; surely the Holy Father is no longer informed of the truth of the matter, for the man of God, our holy Pope, would grant us everything.3 Patience! Everything will come to light, but I remain resigned in God!

4. Listen, my Monsignor, returning to the girl: if you want to send her here to Piacenza, do so; the House of Saint Anne is always ready to receive anyone who comes with a note from Your Excellency, so indebted to you am I in gratitude.

5. I would ask you a favour. I would like to have His

Holiness bless a Genoese priest, Don Biale, nephew of the Bishop of Ventimiglia, who is gravely ill and entrusted to our care here in Piacenza and would like before he dies to receive the blessing of the Holy Father.4 Please convey it to him with a line of your own.

I assure you it would bring great consolation to the poor sufferer, and I am sure I shall receive, before he dies, a letter from you bearing that blessing.

6. I thank you in advance together with the said Priest who makes the request. I ask for your Apostolic blessing, while I remain with the greatest veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble Servant Sr. ANNA M. ROSA GATTORNO

1 the girl you recommend. A poor girl named Olimpia, whom a brother of his wanted to place in the Trastevere house, but not to prepare her for a post as a domestic servant, and whom the ladies of the Pious Union refused.

2 My right arm: Fr Tornatore. Despite her requests (cf. L 68;

89;) she had not managed to obtain his readmission.

3 She was told that everything depended on the Holy Father, but she thought otherwise.

Cf. L 134, n. 2.

4 Don Biale: cf. L 742,4.

She is sorry to hear of her many troubles and would gladly take them on herself. Everything for the Lord is little; she is not to be downcast. She has the Countess answered, explaining why the girls do not enter the College: not the cost, but the lack of air and garden. She will send the book the teacher needs.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter and hear how distressed you are, and I am very sorry. I would like to take all your troubles from you and make them mine, adding them to the others; a little more, a [little] less, one suffers just the same.1

2. I hear about the sick Sisters and am very sorry; even more about Stella, which would be a great complication if she got worse. Patience!2

3. Everything for the Lord. You see, my dear, this is the true road to Paradise and to our God. Dear daughter, for Jesus everything is little. Come, courage, don't be downcast; remember that we are on the cross, because we embraced the cross as our inheritance. We do what we can on our part, and the rest we must leave to God, for he can do everything and we nothing.3

4. Today I also received a letter from the Countess — whom Sr. A. Vincenza is answering right now — telling me to tell you that you accept girls without asking them to bring the 50 F. entry fee. For your information, I am having her told that it is not the 50 F. that holds parents back from placing their girls there, but another reason.4

5. Then when girls come to enter and you cannot come to terms, and they too act like the others because there is no garden or air, write frankly to the Countess, so that she sees why girls do not enter.5

6. For the rest, about the vows, do as you think best, but you must not listen to the devil; you have enough sense and instruction in spiritual matters to know that the devil envies our good and always tempts us to hold back from it.6

7. Goodbye; I commend Sr. A. Irene to you; I hope Sr. A. Beatrice's illness is nothing serious, and the cook's too; cheer her up, tell her to take heart and not dwell on her illness but try to drive away melancholy.7

8. Tell the teacher that the teacher Onorata told me those books are enough to obtain the elementary diploma. As for Carpigiani's book, it was Sr. A. Vincenza's mistake when she sent them; she didn't know she was to put that book in the trunk too, but I'll send them soon.8

Goodbye, (your) God bless you and the Community.

Affectionate MOTHER

1 The previous day's letter was truly not consoling because of the sad news. The Mother sympathizes with her daughter, ready to take on all her sadness and add it to her own many troubles.

2 The sick: two Sisters and a girl, Stella, sister of Sr. A. Panasia, who had had a fever for four days.

3 At this point she gradually leads the disheartened Superior to reason from the standpoint of faith and of the call to follow Jesus in complete abandonment, like him, to the Father's will.

4 The real reason is not the entry fee but another: the unsuitability of the premises.

5 Here she says clearly: the lack of a garden and of adequate ventilation in the rooms.

6 Regarding the religious vows. Sr. A. Paola had written: "I wanted to make my vows... but my heart is so sad that I could not savour them, so I am putting it off until the Immaculate Conception".

7 Sr. A. Irene Calmeli, a postulant in the Ferrara house, had received the habit there on 4 October. (Cf. Letters to the Mother from Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti, 1, 2, 5 October

1873).

8 The lay teacher asked for more books to prepare some Sisters for obtaining the elementary teaching diploma. But the teacher Onorata Colli had told her that they were sufficient. Lisetta Carpegiani was the other lay teacher in Ferrara.

Every day she blesses the Lord, who loves her and guides her with special lights. Courage: one day they will be together for eternity in full joy. She would like her to write her mother a fine affectionate letter and console her by expressing the beauty of the state she has embraced.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I reply at once to your letter, received together with those of the two teachers, Sr. A. Adelaide and Sr. A. Dorotea, which I assure you were no small consolation; and I am answering Sr. A. Adelaide with a line.1

2. Listen, my dear daughter, this poor Mother of yours blesses the Lord for you every day, seeing how much he loves you; one can always see that he inspires you, since you answer these gentlemen so aptly and according to my intentions.2

3. Courage, daughter, for one day we shall be together for an eternity of joy; there the torments will be over, our sufferings ended, joy alone will be our inheritance; ever united we shall taste the fruit of the blood shed [and] the sweat of our labours.3

4. Listen, my beloved, I would like you to write to your Mother and two lines to Signora Maria, but I want them to be all honey, telling them many lovely, consoling words about the state you have embraced and the consolation you feel.4 I won't go on describing what to say, for I see well how good you are at expressing yourself; and give them your address, saying you would like often to be blessed by your mother. Put this on the address: To the Superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne Carlotta Biagini, Rimini for Pennabilli.

5. As soon as your things arrive5 I shall send them with Sr. A. Adelaide's shifts; I am waiting so as to make one parcel. Goodbye, my dear daughter; the Lord bless you and the others, while I hold you always in Jesus, your

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini and Sr. A. Dorotea Benedetti.

2 On the 27th the Sister had told her she had spoken with the President and the Mayor about the need for two more religious to nurse the sick,

since the others were busy with the school. Cf. L 138,4.

3 Courage... one day we shall be together. The distance weighed on the Daughter. She had written in the same letter: "My thoughts, dear Mother, night and day are turned to you, and I cannot help shedding a tear when I think that I am so far from you, for it is so far; but still, meanwhile I am much consoled by your letters and so I shall try to do everything as you wish".

4 Signora Maria Grampini: cf. L 12, n. 3. Her mother, Signora Giovanna, still could not understand how her Nanetta (as they called her), who had left Foligno with the Mother for Rome and then Piacenza (cf. L 110,1; 112,4;

120, n. 3), had then decided to join the FSA. Anna Biagini had received the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne on 30 September 1873.

5 Her mother had not yet sent her outfit.

She is not to worry about nursing the sick. If people come asking for the Sisters, she should answer that it is not possible, as the Sisters are busy with the Schools. Patience; crosses are inevitable. The Mother will go to Genoa.

A.M.F.

My beloved daughter,

1. I have just received your letter and hear what you did with the Bishop. Listen, my dear, for now say no more about it, and without saying anything don't overwork yourselves; do only what belongs to your office; and if (gli) they come asking for the sick, answer politely: "I am very sorry, but we cannot, because we are all busy with the schools".2

2. As for the teacher, be patient; I understand all your distress, but what can you do? The Lord wills it so; one must be resigned. If you didn't have this, you would certainly have other crosses, and perhaps heavier ones.3

3. Don't be surprised about the confessor, for it happens everywhere.4 My dear, you see, I wrote to you yesterday and again today to reply at once to yours and at the same time let you know that on Monday I am going to Genoa; address your letters there: Vicolo San Donato No. 4, 2nd floor.5

Goodbye, for I am in a hurry, and I don't know if you'll understand this writing.

[your Affectionate MOTHER ROSA GATTORNO]

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 With the Bishop. She had asked him to plead their cause so that the Mother might send two more Sisters to help nurse the sick at home. Cf. L 138,4.

3 As for the teacher: Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini. Cf. L 138, n. 2. She was ill, rather frail, and needed much patience and understanding.

4 The confessor. He would linger at the house chatting.

5 On Monday I am going to Genoa: 3 November.

She is greatly consoled to hear that they love one another and that peace reigns among them. She urges her to look after her health and see that the Sisters' food is good and wholesome. She asks for news of her mother: whether she has written to her and how she took the news that she is Superior in Pennabilli.

A.M.F.

My beloved daughter,

1. Just a line to tell you I hear the teacher is in better health; so give her meat, but in the evening always give her what you give her now. She loves you very much and only wants to know whether you are pleased, whether you love her and whether her conduct pleases you.2

2. Believe me, daughter, this Sister of yours is very fond of you and wants nothing but to satisfy all your wishes.3

3. God be blessed! What consolation I feel when I hear that peace reigns among you. May God keep it for you; poor as I am, every day I pray good God to grant it to you.

4. Dear daughter, how is your health? Has your toothache gone, does it still hurt? Take care of yourself, for charity's sake; see that the food is wholesome and good, meat as I wrote, and a little [undiluted] wine when needed; our Rules forbid it, but when it is necessary to drink it strong, it may be done.4

5. Courage, my daughter, for one day you will be happy, and I hope to hear it from your lips as well as in writing.

6. How did your mamma take the news you gave her that you are Superior of Pennabilli? I would like to know something; I can imagine Signora Maria; I hope she was pleased.5 I would have liked Sr. A. Augusta to write to her in the same vein as I told you to, but what can you do, I cannot get her to; patience!6 I would like her to change her character and take on humility, the treasure of all treasures, but I have not yet succeeded.

God bless you, and believe me your

affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the letters she is answering (one from Sr. A. Carlotta of

2.11, the other from Sr. A. Adelaide of 6.11).

2 She had already written about how to treat Sr. A. Adelaide. Cf. L 138,1.

3 With great tact she dispels doubts and misunderstandings.

4 In every letter she repeats the same advice, because she likes to hear that her daughters are well physically and morally. Cf. L 135,6.

5 Cf. L 144,4.

6 Sr. A. Augusta, her sister, who had preceded her in her vocation among the Daughters of Saint Anne. But she had an independent character.

She may ask for her embroidery and other things, but with gentleness, charity and humility. This virtue is the greatest of treasures.

A.M.F.

My beloved daughter,

1. I was slow to answer yours, my dear; I am so busy I don't know what to do. Listen, you ask whether you may ask Signora Maria for your embroidery and other things. Yes, my dear, do so, always gently, and although you know they are yours and belong to you by right, I want you to ask for them as a favour.1

2. Yes, my dearest, this pleases the Lord. He loves humility so much. Ah! my treasure, when shall I possess you? Humility! Humility! Treasure of all treasures!2

3. Courage; do as I tell you and you will see you will be glad. Goodbye, greet everyone, and receive many greetings in the Heart of Jesus, where I hold you and remain for life your

affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 The Sister had asked in her letter of 2 November. Maria Grampini, cf. L 144,4.

2 The Lord loves humility: "take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls"

(Mt 11:29-30).

The Father will already have told her to send the religious, so she should see to it and give them the personal belongings the Mother needs. Her relatives have sent her a little providence: she is to thank them. Saint Anne and the Eternal Father will not let her lack what the house needs.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I have just received yours and hear how ill Don Biale is.1 Let us leave everything to the Lord. I hope the Father had a good journey and told you to send the religious; at first we had agreed on four; this morning I heard Don Accinelli said three; so if this reaches you in time, keep the one at Poss, Sr. A. Costanza,2 and send the others at once.

2. You did well to put all Annetta's things in order and keep them; when I come we shall see to everything;3 when the religious come, send me our shoes, the wool-lined ones, and our overcoats, including Sr. A. Vincenza's of course.

3. I am glad your father and the others have sent something. Be sure to thank them, so that they remember us another time, and besides it is our duty. I hope Saint Anne and my Eternal Father will send you all you need. Trust in God and you will see that whoever trusts in him obtains (si) everything.4

4. For charity's sake, I commend Don Biale to you; be patient; with patience everything is obtained.

5. Courage, for we are truly in the storms; let us pray fervently and unceasingly, and dear God will hear us; so he will not be slow to send you the providence the house needs.5

6. Don't forget to have the girl from Nizza seen about the tumour she has. It would be good to have it cut out, so she is rid of it sooner; putting it off it could become serious; for now another...6

Goodbye, believe me your p.

Affectionate MOTHER ROSA

1 Don Biale. Cf. L 142,5.

2 Fr Tornatore had been in Genoa for the "Ricchini case". "keep the one at Poss":

Sr. A. Costanza Cenni was with the working girls at the Poss factory.

3 Annetta's things, that is, Sr. A. Carlotta Biagini's. Cf. L 144, n. 5.

4 She had received various gifts in kind: Marchioness Marianna Anguissola 400 faggots of firewood, her father two sacks of maize and one of fodder, Signora Laura Scopesi chestnuts.

She apologizes that Carlottina did not invite him to spend a few days in Piacenza: she has been under treatment in Genoa for her hearing. She answers about the Institute's activities. For further references the priest concerned could apply to the Bishop or to Prefect Binda of Piacenza.

Reverend Director,

1. I have received your esteemed letter here in Genoa, where I have been for a few days. First of all, Carlottina's apologies for not having had the pleasure, as she ardently wished, of begging Your Reverence to come and spend a few days in Piacenza, together with the most worthy teachers.1 The reason was the treatment she began for her hearing with a doctor here in Genoa, from which she feels some benefit, so that she had to forgo that great consolation.2 Your Reverence wishes for news of God's work, and I am glad to give it as it stands.

2. In these years we already number fifteen Houses and are negotiating for many others.3 We have charge of Hospitals, with Infant Schools, day Schools for boys and boarding schools for girls. Not to mention home nursing, which gives us a vast field for the exercise of charity, since we are much sought after for it;4 for further information, the most worthy Priest you mention could apply to the Bishop or to the Prefect of Piacenza, Cavaliere Binda.

3. At present I am in Genoa, where we have a house of our Order, and I am about to open another on the Western Riviera.5 I shall stay here about twenty days; if Your Reverence has anything for me, I give you my address so that letters may reach me safely, even if I am away on business, never staying long in one place.

Please accept Carlotta's kindest regards together with mine, and kindly convey them to the excellent lady Teachers, while I remain with every esteem Your Reverence's

Most humble Sr. ANNA M. R. GATTORNO

1 I have received yours. It is dated 9.11.1873 and tells her that a priest friend of his intends to found in Milan a work for home nursing, and asks for news of her Congregation. (AFSA, 95, 1864-1877, n. 14). In the years when Carlotta was a boarder at the "Institute for the Deaf and Dumb" he directed in

Milan, she used to invite him and the Teachers to Piacenza.

2 Carlotta had been under treatment for her hearing for several months. Cf. Rapallino letters of

1873 to M. Rosa.

3 Cf. L 139,1.

4 In almost all the houses the Sisters also took on home nursing of the sick.

5 At Sestri Ponente.

She replies point by point to two letters about a girl who should leave and is ill, and about her own ever precarious health.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your two letters; in the last I hear that the good Countess is coming to stay with you.1 Give her my warm regards.

2. As for the girl: when she is somewhat better, but no longer with Sr. A. Beatrice, so that, this Sister being better, nothing is disturbed.2

3. As for troubles: my dear, it is the same everywhere;3 do everything you can for Stella, for it would be a bad business if she died; her stubborn illness worries me. Ah! if only she could be brought to Piacenza, I assure you I would be glad.4 As for my health: it is poor. What can you do? The pain never leaves me and I breathe with great difficulty. Let us leave everything to good God. Have your girls and nuns pray hard for a very important matter.5 Goodbye, I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA. God bless you, and always believe...

1 Of 7 and 10 November respectively. The good Countess: Maria Anna

Trotti, who from time to time stayed at Palazzo Obizzi, which she had given to the

FSA.

2 As for the girl Stella, Sr. A. Panasia's sister, who was ill: as soon as she is fit to travel she may have her accompanied to Piacenza, but not by Sr. A. Beatrice, who is convalescent and had better not undergo such strain.

3 As for troubles — worry about the Countess's coming and others —

she assures her they are daily bread in the other communities too.

4 The Superior wrote that her illness was stubborn; she had been in bed for a month and, despite doctors' visits and treatment, could not shake it off.

5 a very important matter: probably the "Ricchini case", since she had been summoned to swear "the oaths" in court. Cf. L 140,5.

She is disappointed that the Father has not written. She may send away the two postulants who want to go home. She is to withdraw Sr. A. Apollonia from Don Biale's and have the dormitories cleaned and tidied. She should see how to obtain some alms. She ought to speak to Poss about the girls and arrange the administration of the house he provides. The Mother is in tribulation: God's will be done.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday the Sisters arrived and gave me your letter. I am sorry to hear the Father had a bad journey;1 I would have thought he would write two lines, but what can you do, I am sadder than ever; I suppose I am neither marchioness nor countess, so I am not worth the trouble of writing.

2. Now to the house: I hear two postulants want to leave; well, I would be for sending them at once, all the more since the one from Cremona eats Saint Anne's bread having brought nothing, so we can keep nothing. So if she says she wants to go, send her quickly, without wasting time, reckoning it is one mouth fewer.2

3. What can I say? The Lord humbles us to atone for our frailties.

4. You tell me you have not yet been able to do anything about the dormitory because Sr. A. Apollonia is at Don Biale's. And do you know what you must do? Don't send her there any more. Say — not using illness as an excuse; it is the truth, all the more since if she continued she would certainly fall seriously ill, as it is a long business. I would like to find them all well arranged, with matching colours on the beds, everything in order.3

5. I can't understand why you say you had to make bodices for the girls, when I saw so many in the linen room. I can't understand the Parish Priest — how distressing! go to the Marchioness and ask her; go again about Lazzero. You know, tell her for charity's sake to ask Mr Perletti to pay the miller's bill,4 and likewise from Poss.5

6. You must not rely on Pastore; see how things stand, and if he says: "I want the forty girls", tell him you will send them when they are well.6 And write to me at once that there are two from Nizza, one with nothing and the other with 12 F. a month; then I can send some of those from S. P. d'Arena.

7. Now I would like to know whether you have any spare woollen blankets of ours, the heavy community ones, because they would like two here; but if you have more, let me know.

8. I hear about Addolorata;7 you did well; my God! what can we do with this creature? You had better let the Superior of Foligno know that you have received Annetta's things, so that she can tell Signora Maria.8

9. Tell Don Biale I have received his letter and am glad about his health.

10. I hear Sr. A. Buon Pastore is rejecting capable girls without Poss saying anything.9 What a thing! It horrifies me, for to think that no one considers the good of the house is heartbreaking. Can't she see that if he says nothing, meanwhile it is one more mouth for us, and she earns nothing? However little she gets, it is always something.

11. For pity's sake let us think it over and try to help ourselves in every way and in those good God sends us; I want to see this carried out: since it is up to us to bear the expenses and they live too grandly, collect the money at once and keep it apart, providing them with everything, so that we can see whether it suffices for their keep.10

12. I hope you gave Sr. A. Giovanna the bodice, and the portress too.11

13. I don't know which way to turn; there are tribulations on all sides, so what can be done? Be resigned to God's will, and be patient! I end by wishing you and the Community a thousand blessings from heaven, while I remain yours. Give my regards to the Father; your

Affectionate M. ROSA

14. Keep the Roman girl ready for me, and the one at Poss, Sr. A. Costanza; I hope to send for them soon.12 I can't understand about Cortemaggiore.13

1 Cf. L 148, n. 2.

2 Financial straits were making themselves felt.

3 Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti, one of Don Giovanni Biale's nurses. "...

it is the truth, all the more since if she continued, certainly": it is the truth, all the more since if she went on with that constant and lengthy work, she would certainly fall seriously ill. I would like to find the dormitories all in good order and with bedspreads of the same colour.

4 Sr. A. Francesca had written that she had no money: "I keep hoping providence will come, but it never does" (L 8.11.1873). The Parish Priest: Don Elia Magnani (cf. L 12, n. 8) had sent her nothing. The Mother advises her to go to various benefactors.

5 Emilio Poss was one of the owners of the Spinning Mill where about forty girls cared for by the Daughters of Saint Anne worked. Cf. Appendix IV.

6 Pastore: Sr. A. Del Buon Pastore Dosi. If Poss insists that the 40 girls be present, as agreed, tell him that when they are well you will send them.

7 Sr. A. Addolorata was not doing her job as cook well, and the Superior had scolded and punished her (L Camisa to M. Rosa 11.11.1873).

8 Annetta, Anna Biagini, now Sr. A. Carlotta. Signora Maria Grampini, a family friend. Cf. L 144,4.

9 capable girls: perhaps she meant: she rejects the less capable girls, leaving them at home. This did not serve the Institute's interests. However little she gets. Even if the rejected girl earned a meagre wage, it was still a help for the house.

10 ...think it over... sends. Let us help ourselves in every way on the occasions good God sends us. Since it is up to us to manage the keep of the girls employed there as workers, collect the wages and manage them by buying what they need; in this way we can see whether the pay they receive is enough for their keep.

11 Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio.

12 Sr. A. Costanza Cenni. The Roman girl, probably one of the postulants from Rome; she would call them to Genoa.

She urges her to look after her health and never to omit Communion. She is sending her some provisions to keep in a separate pantry. A Sister will return from Ferrara and can be sent to Nizza; likewise she will send two more if the request comes from Ovada.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear from yours that you are short of breath. Listen, my dear daughter, will you give me a great consolation — to look after your health and be able to write to me that your cough is going, that you are eating and are cheerful? Everything else we shall place in the Heart of God the Father. And make your Holy Communion every day.1

2. Ah! what contentment to be united to good God; but you, my dear, if you stay away from this dear and most loving One, you will never have anything, I fear. Go, go and suck the honey of sweetness! He is its very essence; so run to his fountain and drink, get drunk. Oh! blessed moment when I see my beloved daughter drunk with this wine.2

3. Now something about yours, received a few hours ago together with one etc.. be cheerful, look after yourself.3

4. I shall have to stay here a long time and may spend Christmas here, but don't worry, you will be just as happy, do you understand me?4

5. Tomorrow I'll send you a barrel of raisins, 8-10 boxes of dried figs, a sack of sugar, and meanwhile I enclose the note on how to make the wine; if you decide to make it, make only a little at a time, a few litres, otherwise it goes bad.5

6. Go to the excise office and to the Town Hall to complain that they open our crates and help themselves. This time I would be very upset, for charity's sake; since these are very costly things, I want you to have them put in the pantry by the main staircase and keep the keys yourself. I have not yet sent the pasta because they cannot dry it, but as soon as there is some I'll send it.6

7. You did well to make a fuss about the bread; Saint Anne will put it in your book of labours.

8. I don't want you to take this letter to its destination yourself, because it is too far and your health suffers, do you understand?7 Nizza is asking me for another nun. Listen, Sr. A. Giulia is coming back from Ferrara, so we shall send her there at once; any day is good for me to call the Sisters, so there will be fewer mouths to feed.8

9. When you have put the dormitory in good order, lock it and keep it locked; tomorrow two girls will reach you from Nizza, so you can send them to Poss; one pays 12 F. Yours for ever

MOTHER [ROSA]

10. P. S. If they come for the nuns for Ovada, give them

Sr. A. Ernesta and the other, Sr. A. Costanza.9

Get this to Sr. A. Buon Pastore at once. Greet all the Sisters; I would like to know how many girls there are in the house.

2 The Mother is firm and persuasive in her teaching.

3 The letter the Mother refers to is missing.

4 you will be just as happy.

5 She advises her to make wine at home.

6 By buying provisions wholesale she saved a good deal.

7 To Fr Tornatore, at the Alberoni College, which was far from the Mother House.

8 There is always a good time to call the Sisters and relieve the Mother

House.

9 Sr. A. Ernesta Savani and Sr. A. Costanza Cenni.

She is not entirely well. She approves what she has done and gives some advice about the house and the transfer of some Sisters. She hopes she has complained to the excise office so that they do not take fruit from the crate she is sending; it costs a great deal.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am answering yours in my own hand. You ask how my health is; I tell you my pain is stubborn and always stops me breathing.

2. Now to what you ask about the postulant with 80 F.: you did well not to accept her; as for the overcoat, you may cut it up, but I want you to cut it yourself, so that we get a little more out of it; for bread, always keep to the second quality.

3. Sr. A. Maddalena will reach you; send her to the Morte, and send the girl to Poss; and as soon as you can, move Sr. A. Gerolama and send her to the Morte infirmary.1

4. I am pleased about the girl.2 The girls at Poss must number 40; I think that is what we said.

Giovanni who doesn't want to stay. I hope you have complained so that they don't touch the fruit you are to receive, for it was sent 5 days ago. Listen, I enclose the recipe for making wine; they drink it here and say it is so good; make it if you like; 4 figs are enough for the girls' supper, for that is what they do here too.6 Go to Marchioness Anguissola as soon as you can.7 I spent 110 F. on this fruit alone. You see how dear it is; take care (ci) of the sugar that will soon reach you. Keep it under lock and key. Goodbye, I am your affectionate M...

Goodbye; I bless you and all the others.

6 Mgr Augusto Negrotto: cf. L 142,1 and 4 and L Sr. S. Cuore Cocchella to

M. Rosa of 16.11.73.

7 Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli Casoni was the Protector of the Institute and Mgr Mariano Wantienkist his Secretary.

She is ill and feverish. Tomorrow the house in Sestri opens. She tells her to keep everything in order, as she will need her. Advice about the accounts.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Today I have not had a minute to write to you. Sr. A. Vincenza [is] at S. P. d'Arena, and at three o'clock I came down with a fever and could no longer stand. My dear daughter, how much illness I carry on my shoulders! it seems impossible that I can stay on my feet.

2. Tomorrow I go to Sestri: at last that house is opening; I shall still need two religious.2

3. Listen, I must warn you that if you make the wine you should put in less sugar than is written, a good third less.3

4. I want to hear soon that everything is finished, in order and locked up on all sides; I may need you, but for pity's sake take care of yourself and your health; don't overdo it, now that there are fewer of you in the house.4 So, courage!

5. You tell me about that postulant; I tell you to accept her; for charity's sake, accept her. You did well to accept the other.

6. Keep Don Biale's accounts carefully; now pay the meat bill at once, and the one at the Morte too; and then keep separate note of all the meat you take for Don Biale.5

7. I don't know how to send Ernesta to Nizza, where they need her so much.6 Mind you don't catch cold. I'll stop, because I want to go to church and to bed, for it is late.

I am your affectionate MOTHER

God bless you, and always yours; Carlotta, who is here, wants me to write that she sends her greetings. Goodbye, goodbye.

1 This letter is headed to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni. But the error is obvious, since she had died on 13 April 1873.

2 At Sestri Ponente. At last: Don Antonio Accinelli had been negotiating since September (Cf. AFSA, AA1M.).

3 Cf. L 152,5; 153,7.

4 Everything in order, so the rooms are locked awaiting the arrival of the incoming postulants. Cf. L 151,4. Fewer of you in the house. Cf. L 153, n. 5.

5 She was to keep separate the accounts of Don Giovanni Biale (cf. L 69, n. 5)

and those of the house in Via della Morte.

6 Cf. L 153, n. 3.

She asks her to get Onorata to find a teacher for the Sampierdarena school, and to send a Sister to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to tell you to send for the teacher Onorata and ask her to find you a teacher qualified for 4th class, and send her to S. P. d'Arena at once.1 See that she is good, not intimidating, and inexpensive.

2. I hear about Sr. A. Giovanna; had she put on the plaster she would have recovered. I hope Buon Pastore is well.2

3. Listen, Sr. A. Apanasia will reach you in Piacenza, and you must send her to Rome. She would like to take her sister.3 Well, who knows, she may come with Sr. A. Vincenza; so, the teacher at once.

4. Today, a day of great pain, my breathing is laboured and I have a slight cough. I write little because my arm hurts.

It will be as God wills. Take care of yourself, for charity's sake; look after your health.

Greet everyone; accept strong, sturdy postulants. Goodbye, I am your affectionate

M[OTHER]

1 Onorata Colli. She turned to her to find young teachers.

2 Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio was ill; Sr. A. Francesca feared it was erysipelas. Buon Pastore Dosi; (Cf. L Sr. A. Francesca 27.11.73).

1 Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi was arriving from the Ferrara house with her sister Stella. (Cf. L 122, n. 2 and 3; 124,3).

Grateful for the many proofs of his fatherly protection, she sends Christmas greetings and assures him of the community's prayers and her own.

My most Reverend Father,

1. Your charitable heart always gives us new proofs of protection. My Father, how indebted I am to you! I pray God to send me an opportunity to show my gratitude better in deeds than in words.2

2. Meanwhile, on Christmas night prayers will rise to good God for you, as will the Sacrifice of Holy Mass. I would like to know, my Father, why this permission is restricted to this House alone and cannot serve for the others?3 Forgive my boldness and bless me; prostrate, I remain with all veneration Your Most Reverend Lordship's

Most humble and devoted Servant Sr. ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The date is inferred from the reply: 4 December 1873.

2 She had asked him to obtain for her the faculty to have Midnight

Mass celebrated in the Institute's Chapels.

3 He replied: "The Congregation of Rites does not grant the faculty for all houses. Perhaps the Briefs office would grant it, but at great expense. I did as I do for our

Monasteries hitherto. One asks for each individually". AFSA, 4, MaR.

She is in Piacenza and will go to Cortemaggiore and then to Genoa. She should speak to the Bishop about the school. When writing to her mother, she should greet the Father Guardian. Be cheerful! The Mother keeps her close.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have received your letter with Sr. A. Adelaide's; you will see that I am in Piacenza; tomorrow I go to Cortemaggiore.

2. Thank you for your prayers; I am very grateful. My dear, I write in haste because I have so much to do; my health? I can barely stand, but your prayers sustain me. Keep it up.

3. As for your answer about the teacher, you did well; and you may take the girls out for walks, telling the Bishop that I want whatever Your Excellency wishes to be done. Only plays I cannot allow. For the rest, tell him the mother wishes them to do Your Excellency's will.1

4. Courage, my dear; when you write to mamma, be sure to greet the Father Guardian.2 You know how good this religious is, and besides, my dear daughter, he is a servant of God and that's enough; you will do it, won't you?

5. I am staying here in Piacenza until the 23rd, then I leave again for Genoa, for your information. Be cheerful and content, for your poor mother keeps you always close to her, that you may become a heroine of virtue and love. Goodbye; you will receive your things; the teacher's will be marked.3

Yours for ever

MOTHER ROSA

1 The President of the Congregation of Charity had several times told her to take the girls to church and sometimes for walks. She agreed;

she was only against their putting on theatrical performances (plays).

2 The Father Guardian of the Franciscan Friars of Foligno, Fr Giuseppe Sensi.

3 The things from her outfit, together with Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini's, distinguishable from hers because they were marked. Cf. L 154,4.

She expresses joy at the news of the audience with the Holy Father. Encouragement and advice. She will send to her house the letters for the Sisters of the Parrocchietta and of Via delle Fornaci, sure that she will forward them promptly.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. You will receive this from Sr. A. Panasia;2 how welcome your letters were, especially the one describing the audience with the Holy Father! Ah! what a great saint our Pope is! What consolation I felt on hearing that he deplores that wretched man's conduct and joins me in my sorrow! Oh! what blessedness of martyrdom you are! Suffering is little when accompanied by such sweet comfort!3

2. My daughter, courage; go on acting prudently and thriftily; I am very pleased with the overcoats you made.

3. The religious coming with Sr. A. Panasia must go straight to the Parrocchietta, and take Sr. A. Ambrogia with you as nurse.

4. Your report is fine; carry on like that; if you have not yet fixed the retreat, you could answer that you will make it when I arrive, as long as you see that Monsignor is not displeased and nothing has been arranged.4

5. If the postulants come, see that they have everything, and their money, so that it doesn't happen as with the one they brought me.

6. The letters I send from now on for the Parrocchietta and the Fornaci I shall send to you, and you will get them to them; Giovanni's stable5 is near you, and the Fornaci too are nearer you. I hope none will be lost and that you will faithfully forward them. For now I have nothing more but to wish you a thousand blessings from heaven, while I am your

P. M. ROSA

7. Greet them all and tell them to pray for me, as I wish them all observant and holy; with the blessing I wish them, I remain theirs

M. R.

1 The draft lacks the addressee, but she is clearly identified by comparing the letters of this period.

2 Sr. A. Panasia Bellardi. Cf. L 122, n. 2.

3 It is dated 16 November, the day of the audience. When the

Superior asked his blessing for her, the Holy Father asked: "she's in Genoa, isn't she? about certain papers. And he added: "sad times, one must suffer, but well, all for the honour of good Jesus". Clearly the Holy Father knew what

Ricchini (that wretched man) had done.

4 The annual Spiritual Exercises may be postponed, as long as you see that

Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist is not displeased and provided you have not already fixed anything.

5 The letters she wrote could be delivered through Giovanni,

the carter they used.

She asks her to press Mr Liberati to send the teacher soon.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line in haste. First, I have received all your letters;1 second, please see that Mr Liberati sends that young qualified teacher soon, and the educated ones too.2

2. Greet all the Sisters. Courage, forward, for one day we shall rest for an eternity.

Goodbye; please press about the teacher, your affectionate M. ROSA. On the 22nd I leave for Genoa.

1 The letters she mentions have not survived.

2 There is no more precise information about Mr Liberati. Perhaps it is Liberali,

a Vincentian, confessor of the Community. From what the Mother says, he had directed young postulants to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

She may give the soup to the servant. If no letters from the Mother arrive, it means she is to return to Piacenza next Saturday.

My daughter,

1. I received the let[ter] this morning, your other one. You may give him the soup you mention, and anything else left over; about the oil you can speak to the archpriest.2

2. If you see no letters from me, come on Saturday, come without fail.3 I shall write if you are to stop at Fiorenzuola to collect that money; you will find the Superior there.

Goodbye, I have visitors. Yours for an eternity, affectionate M. R.

1 She replies to a letter of Sr. A. Vincenza of 16.12.1873.

2 She asked whether she could give the servant Giovanni the soup prepared for the hospital.

3 Come on Saturday, that is, the 20th.

She thanks her for her letter. The Community prays for her every day. She asks her not to forget the needs of the Work, which is spreading to comfort so many neglected girls and unfortunate people. She asks in particular for her help, as she must prepare a Chapel for the new House and has nothing. She ends with Christmas and New Year greetings.

Most esteemed Marchioness,

1. I can assure you, dear Marchioness, that the words of your letter were extremely dear and vivid to me. Be sure that never a day passes without this Community raising prayers for you; and you, good Marchioness, do not forget us, who are so very poor, especially now that we have a new house to open in Milan2 which, for lack of very little means, we cannot yet occupy. Here in Rome there is extreme need because of the multitude of neglected daughters growing up left to themselves,3 and other unfortunates who die without the help and comfort of Religion.4

2. We already have a small part of a House, but it cannot be lived in, as it is so arranged that, being occupied by other owners, we cannot enter.5

3. My Marchioness, this House has no Chapel, no furnishings, nothing,6 and I, like my Jesus' poor donkey, go seeking to furnish my Jesus' House, and those few furnishings, so that there too the Sacrifice of Holy Mass may be offered to the august Trinity. Please, Marchioness, put in a word with that blessed lady of the Abbey of Tor de' Specchi

? 296

so that she too may offer some cupboard and, if need be, some less precious object, and give it to this poor house of Jesus.7

4. Forgive me if I keep troubling you with my tiresome letters, but you know better than I that when it comes to adorning so august a dwelling nothing else comes to mind, for this thought devours everything else.

Please accept my wishes for happiness and many blessings from heaven for the feasts of Holy Christmas and for the coming year.

Most humble Sr. ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO

1 The addressee is missing, certainly a Lady of the Roman nobility, but there is not enough information to identify her. The date is inferred from the content.

2 Cf. L 149, n. 1 and 170,7.

3 Here in Rome. Perhaps an allusion to the Trastevere house, where

poor girls were housed and trained as domestic servants.

4 She means the poor sick, neglected or not properly cared for by their families.

5 Houses that could not be opened because still occupied by tenants.

6 This house: mentioned in paragraph 1, n. 3.

7 That blessed lady: cf. L 38. n. 1.

She blesses God for the consoling letters received. She urges her to give Christmas and New Year greetings to the Bishop and the President, and to tell the latter that she will send him two more Sisters.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Two lines in haste. First, to tell you I have received yours together with the teacher's.1 God be blessed, for both were consoling.

2. You ask whether to let her go to confession, that is, call the confessor; tell her you cannot and that I wrote to you that I cannot allow it, since our Rules forbid it; so surely she will be satisfied.2

3. I enclose the receipt for the trunk, in case you have not yet received it, though I hope rather that you already have it, since it was sent three days ago.3

4. For charity's sake go to the Bishop to wish him a happy Christmas and New Year, and the President too. Tell him I am glad to be able to send him another Sister for only 150 F., but that I shall send two; [for] one they will pay nothing, because we must go two by two and one would not be enough; so we shall keep the second at our own expense. I shall have the Bishop and the President written to as well.4

Goodbye, my dear, I am in a hurry; greet everyone and believe me your affectionate MOTHER R. G.

5. Don't forget to write a letter of greetings to Father Tornatore. Goodbye; when you have two beds ready, write and I shall send you the two Sisters.

Yours for ever [...]

1 Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini.

2 You ask... that is, call the Confessor. On 14.12.73 she had written:

"She keeps telling me to send for him because she has forgotten some sin".

3 She had already sent her things. Cf. L 161, n. 3.

4 The President Luigi Piccini had at last agreed to receive another

Sister and pay for her, but the Mother sent a second without asking for any payment, since in home nursing the Sisters always went in pairs. Cf. L 138,4.

It is right that they should have a free room for meeting. She is glad they will have Mass on Christmas Night. She is to tell the Superiors of the other houses to write greetings to the Father and go together to receive the Cardinal Protector's blessing.

A.M.F. Daughter,

1. Last night I received your letter and reply at once to what you ask.2 First: it is only right that you should have a free room you can lock and meet in, so I do not at all allow it to be given up; hold firm to what I say. If that Lady wants to come, tell her she must live in the passage room; otherwise she had better go.3

2. Stand firm about the Mass; indeed I am very glad it is to be celebrated that night with a procession,4 always discreetly and quietly, so as not to attract attention, especially at times like these.5

3. Please let the Superiors of the other houses know they are to write a letter of greetings to the Father.6 Understood? You too. I don't need one, for your letters are very dear to me when you give me news of the house and ask me what to do.

4. I am in a great hurry; don't forget to meet all four together and go to receive the Cardinal Protector's Blessing.7 Greet them all and tell them I am not writing to them because I am too busy; I shall write from Genoa, where I return on the 22nd. Write to me there.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you, your affectionate M. R.

I shall soon send you a little money.

1 This letter was assigned to Sr. A. Vincenza Rapallino, but it is clearly for Sr. A. Del S. Cuore Cocchella, for internal and external reasons.

Cf. L 157, n. 1.

2 The letter received is dated 17 December '73.

3 The matter is this: a lady in Rome had asked to be accepted as a paying guest by the Sisters. If she were accepted, the Community would have to give up its small meeting room. The Mother disagrees and suggests taking her in provided she is content with a passage room

(pasaligio).

4 Firm about the Mass. She does what she can to have it celebrated at home on

Christmas night.

5 Times of bitter hostility towards Religious. "Every day they suppress convents and monasteries"; in the streets they insult us, the same Superior had written.

6 The Superiors of the other three Rome houses were to send Christmas greetings to

Fr Tornatore.

7 Cardinal Luigi Vannicelli.

Amid great difficulties and sufferings it is a relief to offer him wishes for prosperity and prayers. The Lord's Work prospers most where it is most opposed. She hopes to be in Rome in February and receive his pastoral blessing for herself and the religious family.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. Every opportunity I have of addressing my most unworthy writing to Your Most Reverend Eminence is no small relief in the stormy sea of tribulations in which I find myself. There is no anguish, no pain, no agony of which my God does not mercifully make me an ample gift; yet in spending a moment with Your Eminence, as though at your feet telling you my wishes for your prosperity, everything is sweetened.

2. I raise most fervent prayers to my Redeemer and long to see Your Eminence filled with every prosperity.

3. The Lord's work is going full sail, and where it is most buffeted, there its Houses spring up larger and more numerous.2

4. With God's help I hope to be in Rome early in February3 and have the good fortune to prostrate myself before Your Eminence and find that word of comfort I have been fortunate enough to hear before, and implore your Pastoral blessing for myself, most unworthy, and for the whole Order of Saint Anne [which in these holy days, Religious and girls prostrate before the sacred Crib of the Child Jesus, offer special prayers for Your Eminence].4

Please accept the homage of one who, full of veneration, kisses your hand and remains most reverently Your Most Reverend Eminence's

Most humble Servant Sr. ANNA M. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The draft (AFSA, 4 MaM, 11) is undated, but the date was noted in the copy book.

2 Cf. L 139. She actually went there on 16 January. The part in [...] is missing from the draft.

Unable to come in person, she sends Christmas greetings. She has opened new houses and a house in Milan is planned. She hopes to come to Rome in February.

Most Reverend Father,

1. Since I cannot have the good fortune of being at your feet and telling you a great many things — for which I would surely find words of comfort in Your Paternity — I must do so in writing, to express the most ardent wishes I make for your prosperity amid the anguish of the present age.

2. May your Christmas be happy and the new year happy too.

3. The reason I have been late in coming there in 1873 is the opening of new houses, now numbering 17, with more about to open.1

4. In the Diocese of Genoa two more were opened, so there are 4 convents there where sorrow weighs on us, but, received in the Heart of Jesus, it is greatly, greatly sweetened.2

5. My Father, man strikes at God's work, and God makes it stronger, spreading it everywhere. Soon we shall be in Milan.3

6. If the move there is not hurried, I hope to be in Rome early in February.4

7. I don't want to weary you with my writing, since however much I wrote I could not convey all I have to tell you in person. Bless me and believe that you have a most wretched Servant who professes obedience to you and remains Your Reverence's

Obl. Most humble Servant Sr. ANNA ROSA GATTORNO

1 Cf. L 139.

2 In the Diocese of Genoa, besides the Sampierdarena Institute, a House had been opened for the School at Sestri Ponente and, at Sampierdarena, the hospital; where sorrow weighs on us alludes to the lack of goodwill of the Archbishop of

Genoa, Mgr Salvatore Magnasco, towards the FSA.

3 Cf. L 149.

4 She went to Rome on 16 January.

She may send the religious, as the railway has been restored. She speaks of some matters and confesses that she lacks money to send her the pasta and for the journey she hopes to make to Milan, where everything is arranged for the opening of a house.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Send the religious, for the tunnel is open again. What a day I had yesterday, my dear, truly seasoned with pepper; patience! all for the Child Jesus.1

2. I could not send you anything because they were not accepting goods; so tell the girls the reason was the railway.2

3. I am glad to hear we can have the medicines; what a resource for our house!3

4. I hope approval has come from Cortemaggiore to send the religious there,4 because here after New Year I shall need her; she would need to learn quickly.

5. And do you know anything more about the Archpriest of Fiorenzuola? What a mess!5 Luckily they could understand nothing from the letter the people of Piacenza opened.

6. I have no money to send you the pasta, because I haven't yet received even that from... Patience! The little I brought from Piacenza I have spent; what Carlotta has is a serious matter, it is so little; if I had to leave at once it would barely be enough, as I also want to stop a [little] at Nizza.

7. And from the letters from Milan I found here, perhaps — indeed certainly — I shall have to go to Milan, as everything seems ready. Would to God

I might go there too! You try to train some Superior for me, otherwise it's a serious matter.6

8. As for the pigs, everything is dear here too, so it will be best to slaughter them. I shall send you the man in mid-January.7 Goodbye; I am just as the Lord wills. God bless you, and believe me always your

affectionate M. R.

1 On the journey to Genoa, because of a train derailment in the tunnel, they had to take a detour, catching a carriage without windows from Busalla to Pontedecimo. Hence a day seasoned with pepper.

2 She had promised the girls something for Christmas, but because of the rail interruption the dispatch office had not accepted the parcel.

3 Cf. L 5.

4 She had recently opened a House at Cortemaggiore.

5 They were negotiating to open a House.

6 Cf. L 149, n. 1. Try to prepare some Superior for me.

7 Pig feed is dear in Genoa too. She will send a man to slaughter them. It is known that they raised a few for household use in the garden of the

Mother House.

She tells her not to send the Sister already assigned to Cortemaggiore. She is to be ready, as the Mother may need her in Genoa; if so, she would accompany that Sister. Before leaving Piacenza she is to leave everything in order.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. If it is still in time, stop sending the widow to Cortemaggiore; instead you could send another, one who is a nurse and can sew; see what you think; if need be, Maria the postulant. Clothe her as best you can and send her; but if (ti) you have already sent the widow, you can exchange them.2

2. I cannot come for New Year. I may need you to come here to S. P. d'Arena.

3. If you are called, you can leave Sr. A. Giovanna in charge for a while and give her clear orders.3 Lock the guest quarters; put all the wardrobe keys in the little room or the cupboard, and those you know they must not open.

4. It is a matter of two or three days; bring the widow with you here to S. P. d'Arena. I hope you have understood; I think I have made myself clear. If the widow has gone to Cortemaggiore, have her relieved, as I say, and keep her ready. And lock the dormitory; in short, whatever you see to be necessary.

5. Tell Sr. A. Nazzarena to be punctual with the coffee and take it to the canon herself; and (le) tell the Canon you are going away for a few days and commend the religious to him, so that if he doesn't see you he will know why, but another will be glad to bring him his coffee.4

6. How many troubles there are, my dear daughter; alas, I feel bowed down on every side; enough! I hope we shall see each other soon and say everything in person. I'm as tired as a pig; I can't go on.

Yours for ever, affectionate M. R.

1 The date is inferred from a letter of Sr. A. Vincenza to Sr. A. Francesca of

29.12.73 dealing with the same matters.

2 It is not known who the widow was who entered the Institute at that time, nor

Maria the postulant. Clothe her as best you can, that is, provide as best you can for her religious clothing.

3 Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio, one of the first five who went to found the Institute in Piacenza.

4 Nazzarena was to bring coffee punctually every morning to Canon Pietro Piacenza, chaplain of the Mother House.

She is to take care of herself. The Mother will send foodstuffs. She invites her to join her in Genoa.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste, for since yesterday I have wanted to answer yours, received with pleasure, but my work is such that it prevents me.

2. For pity's sake take care of yourself, and tell Francesca so; tell her too that Marchioness Anna is coming,2 everything is decided, and that I am sending her two quintals of pasta — let her weigh it when it arrives — and a supply of coffee.3 Tell her to have a new mat put in the little room and the whole house cleaned.

3. I hope she has had the lamp put in the Church for the Canon.4 I shall also send her some zelito and some stockfish. I'll see about a jar of anchovies, and two pairs of shoes for the little girls.5

4. Come on Saturday as early as you can. I am very sorry not to have you here, with so much to do.

5. I'm sending you this sheet; it is for Don Biale.6 Give my regards to that person7 and the Superior, and everyone. Antonietta — for charity's sake, see that she stays.8

Goodbye, I'm in a hurry, I don't know if you'll understand. Goodbye to all, your most affectionate M. ROSA
