Place, day and month are unobjectionable, but the year is problematic. It cannot be checked, as the envelope is missing, but there are precise reasons to date the letter to 1874: first the place — the Mother was in Genoa in January; and the content refers to people and events of January 1874, e.g. Marchioness Anna Carrega's entry into the Institute and other important contextual details.

2 Marchioness Anna Carrega had decided to join the Daughters of

Saint Anne.

3 She was having the pasta and coffee sent, bought wholesale in Genoa to save money.

4 The Canon: Don Pietro Piacenza, chaplain of the Mother House since 1871.

5 She tried to meet the Community's needs by seizing every good opportunity to buy at a good price.

6 Cf. L 142,5.

7 Cf. L 2, n. 3.

8 Perhaps the postulant Antonia Garaviglio of Nizza Monferrato, presented by the Parish Priest Ludovico Bisio. Cf. Reg. Post. n. 228.

She is to send Sr. A. Maddalena to Ovada with a Sister as companion if she does not feel able to travel alone. The Mother will return to Piacenza in a few days; she is to let the Father know.

A.M.F.

My dear Franceschina,

1. Listen carefully: you must send Sr. A. Maddalena to Ovada;1 you can send another with her, who meanwhile will go to learn and then come back after a while.2

2. See whom you can clothe; let her be docile and good; she will make the retreat where she is going, for Don Tito will soon give it.3 Understood? Tell Sr. A. Maddalena to do well; the air there will soon restore her; she is going for the accounts and should do her best.

3. If she is able to go alone as far as Novi, you can write to the Superior to come and fetch her at Novi.4 I leave it to you to do as you think best.

4. For pity's sake, let the house be in order. I am in a great hurry; I hope to be in Piacenza on Tuesday; on Wednesday that person arrives;5 tell him I want to find him at the house, because we shall arrive at 10 in the morning; understood? Goodbye; how ill I feel, dear daughter; last night at 9\ I had a convulsion, like the one I had in Piacenza; and my pain is very bad. I have no more time.

Goodbye, your affectionate

M. [ROSA]

1 Sr. A. Maddalena Terzaghi.

2 The Sister accompanying her may stay a while in that hospital for some training.

3 See whom you can clothe. The clothing of 7 postulants took place on 14

January. Let her be docile and good: the one among those recently clothed who was to accompany Sr. A. Maddalena would make the Spiritual Exercises at Nizza, preached by Don Tito Borgatta.

4 If she can travel alone as far as Novi Ligure, you can write to the

Superior Giacomina Schenardi to go and fetch her.

5 Tuesday 7 January; on Wednesday Fr Tornatore arrives.

She is at last in Rome, after suffering on the journey. If money arrives, she is to pay the debts. She hopes God the Father will provide. She is to leave the house in order. The postulant is admitted to the clothing.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here we are in Rome at last, having arrived yesterday evening at 63 after much suffering — gracious suffering, you who always keep me company. We have not yet received any letters from you (rni); I expected to find some, and the receipt to collect the trunks. I shall soon send you the two postulants, and you'll see: one is a good superior, as dear as can be.2

2. Dear Francesca, for charity's sake, if money arrives pay my bills; you cannot imagine what a consolation it would be! There are also the 200 F. to give to Albertazzi, enough.3 I hope you will have everything through the goodness of God the Father in this his holy month.4 "Yes, my beloved Eternal Father!" Cheer up, we'll see each other soon; meanwhile see to the house, which we left in such disorder. Have the guest quarters and every part cleaned well, and see to the pigs so that nothing goes to waste. I urge you to lock everything up, especially the silver. I told you my intentions before leaving, so I hope you will soon write that all is in order.

3. You may clothe this postulant at once, for she is truly good. I await news of Antonietta; I want to know soon how she is and whether she is happy.5

Goodbye, my dear; I am yours for ever

[MADRE ROSA]

1 The date follows from the context: having left Piacenza on the 13th, she had stopped in

Bologna with Countess Maria Anna Trotti and reached Rome on the 15th.

2 The Reg. Post. lacks the names of the two Roman postulants who entered in January 74; one had the ability to be a good superior.

3 Sante Albertazzi was the doctor of the two Piacenza Communities.

4 The month of January was dedicated with special prayers to the Eternal

Father.

5 The postulant from Rome mentioned in paragraph 1. I await news of Antonietta,

cf. L 172, n. 8.

If the Bishop wishes the pupils to put on the play, she is to agree; the Mother approves whatever he wants. She is to pray that all goes well in Rome, take care of herself and see to the Sisters' food.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here I am in Rome; I didn't answer your letter because I wanted to write to you in my own hand. You asked me about the plays: well, if Monsignor wants them, do as he wishes, for I shall approve whatever His Excellency tells you to do.1 Tell him I agree to all his wishes; he is truly your Father; what an Angel!

2. So write to me here; this is my address: Tor de' Specchi N. 2.

3. I hope you are all well; I didn't stop at all in Foligno, as I was in a hurry to come here.

4. Have prayers said and pray that I may obtain everything,2 and I promise that on my way back I'll come to see you and stay with you a while. The accounts were very good and I am pleased; now you needn't give them to me again until next year.

5. Well done; always forward with courage and in Jesus, clinging tightly to Him, living for Him, dying for Him.3 I am pleased too about poor Augusta. Give my regards to Sr. A. Adelaide and the other two.4

6. Tell Sr. A. Dorotea to eat between meals too, not to let her stomach suffer. Do try to encourage eating between meals, because when teaching it is hard to be at meals; and if you see the teachers need neat wine, you may give it to them. And you, my dear daughter, take care of yourself, eat; and the poultry we were given, eat it, for it will nourish you more than pulses.5

7. I am waiting only for you to tell me the Bishop is calling the other two religious.6 They are ready, two good nurses; you'll be pleased. Keep out of the cold, for charity's sake; light a fire.

Goodbye, my dear, and believe me

your affectionate M. R. God bless you and the others.

1 Cf. L 161,3.

2 Regarding the approval of the Rules.

3 living for Him... dying. Clinging to Jesus, held close to Him so that

He becomes the sole object of her living and acting. Cf. Gal 2:20.

4 Poor Augusta is the sister of the Superior Carlotta. Sr. A. Adelaide

Cervini and the other two Sisters of the house: Sr. A. Dorotea Benedetti and Alessandrina

Lodola.

5 Cf. L 135,6; 136,5; 138,5.

6 Cf. L 166, n. 4; 138,4.

She approves all she has done regarding Poss. The postulant from Rome will arrive soon. Carlotta is ill. She will write to the Father about the outcome of the Rules.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. I have just received your letter and hasten to reply; you did everything right with Poss. Listen: as for the sheets, you can accept his making all the sheets; this once, that is all I can grant him and all I can do; otherwise, stand firm.1

2. What you wrote to her will now cause a muddle in Genoa, because I agreed they should give only 100 F.; so you can write that nothing more is needed, otherwise there'll be a muddle.2

3. I note what you say about the postulant too. Listen: I'll send you this one soon, and she will surely come with Sr. A. Lucia.3 The trunks haven't arrived yet. I hope you'll tell me something soon.

4. I can imagine the work you've had, since we left the house so upside down to be put right. My dear, things are soon done; you know what is hard work? men's heads. Ah, what suffering!

Carlotta is ill, and I fear she may get meningitis; she is very low.

Goodbye, I'm in a hurry, your

Affectionate and ever Affectionate M. R.

God bless you and everyone, and tell them to pray. Goodbye again; tell that person I shall write to him tomorrow evening, because tomorrow is Consistory day for me.4

1 In her letter of 15 January Sr. A. Francesca had explained in detail her talk with Emilio Poss about fitting out the dormitories for the working girls. He was to provide sheets, straw mattresses, blankets and also the bed.

2 It will be a muddle. To satisfy E. Poss, Sr. A. Francesca had asked the Superior in Genoa whether she could give the beds of the girls leaving the Institute.

3 I shall send you this one, i.e. another (cf. L 174,1) from Rome.

4 tomorrow is consistory for me. She may mean that there was to be the plenary session of the S. Congregation of BB and RR to deal with the question of the Rules, or else that she would be called to confer with the competent

Authorities.

Recommendations on observance and various instructions. She asks her to find out from Alessandro whether he has received her letters.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I have received your letters and note what you say about Gregoria,2 and about the begging round; you did well.

2. I urge observance on you, for charity's sake; silence; and try to be present at all community acts, for so you will keep true order — at recreation and other important acts, such as in the morning.3

3. The one at Sestri writes that she needs a nurse, so it would be good, in agreement with Don Accinelli, to send her Sr. A. Alfonsa at once,4 because even when I send her the teacher, she can never act as nurse, since teachers don't do night watches; tell her so. .

4. Tell Don Accinelli too to send me the note of all the privileges I asked him for, which we need for our chapels.5

5. For the rest, I am glad to hear of the subscriptions and all the other alms.6

6. I don't know: I have written twice to Alessandro and he hasn't answered. Find out whether he has received my letters. Tell the one at Sestri I shall write to her soon.

Goodbye; greet all the Sisters for me, in7

[...]

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 Sr. A. Gregoria Sili had received some cloth, and Don Accinelli wanted it because he needed it (cf. letter of Accinelli to M. Rosa 10.1.74).

3 While approving the Superior's going on the begging round, she urges her punctual presence at community acts.

4 The one at Sestri: Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni. In agreement with Don Accinelli

(cf. L 2, n. 4) send Sr. A. Alfonsa Belingeri.

5 The copy of the privileges and faculties granted by the Holy Father Pius IX on 24.1.1866

to the Institute's chapels (AFSA, 81, SSF).

6 Already 66 people had pledged to the subscription for the Genoa

House, which would yield about 1,000 francs a month (letter of Accinelli).

7 The letter was not finished.

She is in Rome; the journey was good; she suffered and felt the help of the "Seraphic Rosa". In the great tribulations she is in, she entrusts herself to God. She is to write and pray, asking Rosa's intercession.

A.M.F.

Most beloved of Jesus and mine,

1. Here I am in Rome; the journey was good but I suffered greatly — only the discomfort which on other occasions, through the intercession of my Seraphic Rosa, I did not suffer at all.1 What an angel of Paradise she is! I send you the address so that you may write me something, for I need it.

2. My dear, I am in great tribulations, alas! God alone sustains me, but all human support is lost to me: what do you think? Write me something; tell me whether I shall come out of it; what shall I do? My head is all upside down when I think of certain things.2

3. I found everything as you told me.3 Only my grace, which I did not receive before coming to Rome — shall I have it? and when? Ah, my Rosa, obtain such a precious gift for me soon!4 Pray and tell me something. As for the postulant and the providence,5 whatever shall I do?

Goodbye, it's late, I'm sleepy and not well, your affectionate

MADRE ROSA

1 She had suffered much, but not the discomfort of other times, through the intercession of her "Seraphic Rosa". Rosa Parodi, a friend of Anna's, who died in the odour of sanctity. Cf. L 389,2.

2 She is speaking of the Rules. She feels unsupported and "all upside down" when she thinks of the situation.

3 Everything... told me. Presumably regarding the houses in Rome.

4 such a precious gift: the approval of the Rules.

5 the postulant. It is not known who she may be. Perhaps Marchioness Anna

Carrega.

She informs her of what she wrote to Mr Poss about organizing the girls' dormitory and what she must do. She points out that, regarding the Sampierdarena hospital, there was a discrepancy with what she must have agreed about payment to the Sisters. They must be more careful.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just received your letter and note what you did about Poss; don't be afraid the Sisters may come to harm;1 I alone wrote to Mr Poss, telling him — I repeat it all for your guidance — that I shall see to everything for the Chapel: chasubles and, in a word, all that is needed. He has only to have the room and altar put in order; I'll see to the rest; let him be quick.2 For the girls I also told him I'll see to the beds, meaning the pillowcases3 and some sheets. He need only help me with the linen, and only once, apart from the pillowcases, which I'll see to, as well as the towels and whatever else is needed. Meanwhile tell him to use the camp beds and so on; the rest will be done slowly; we'll see to the covers; mattresses will be made too, and point out to him that mattresses we make of tow will cost him very little, and by using the camp beds he will spend much less, since no straw mattress is needed.

2. You can see whether you have spare wooden beds, now that there are no more postulants, and you can supply him with those too; tell him: "For the time being everything will do; later, between us, you'll see we'll do better; for now we must manage as best we can." Tell him too that little by little I'll make the white bedspreads, even at my own expense; I hope he'll be satisfied. What more am I to do?

3. I am also writing to Accinelli, for I hear they have made a fine muddle for me. Patience! For charity's sake, [think] before writing, because when agreements have been made, everything else goes well.4

4. Don't be upset that I write to you like this, for you know well that I do it to teach you; I hope you'll understand it so, and be convinced once and for all that my office requires me to do so.5 Goodbye;

now you won't complain any more; I write to you every day.

5. I hope that out of the 700 F. you received6 you have paid the oil bill and the two hundred F. 200 to the miller; for it is

400 F. for the oil bill and [another] two hundred, making 600. You still have a hundred left for yourself. Don't be upset if I do the sums of the money for you, but you know it's my way, and besides I write to you as if I were speaking to you in person.7 Now I can't go on. Goodbye, your affectionate

M. [ROSA]

The Lord bless you and everyone. I am pleased with Antonietta.8

The trunks have not yet arrived.

1 The letter is of 16 January. Sr. A. Francesca had taken the four religious to the Poss factory and, seeing that the beds prepared for them were narrow and uncomfortable, had asked for them to be changed. M. Rosa comments: don't be afraid they may come to harm in uncomfortable beds.

2 He need only have the premises and altar put in order.

3 ...the pillowcases; he is to cooperate by providing at first the sheets and towels. Let him provide the camp beds; we will make the mattresses. By using the camp beds he will spend less, since no straw mattresses are needed.

4 ...a fine muddle. The Superior Francesca had written to the Superior

Santina Solenghi to enquire about the cost of beds, cloth for sheets and straw mattresses, and Don Accinelli had looked into it in detail. The Mother warns her to weigh things carefully before making agreements.

5 Don't be upset... She must teach them how to act in such cases.

6 The Municipality had sent a "warrant" for L. 500 and another for L. 200

for four girls who were to enter the Institute.

7 as if in person: the phrase suits her style perfectly.

8 Antonietta: cf. L 172, n. 8; 174,3.

She is glad to hear part of the debt has been paid; the good God will help with the rest. Let us pray for this and for the other needs, always ready to do his will.

A.M.F.

My Franceschina,

1. Just now — or rather hours ago — I received your letter1 and hear you guessed my wish to pay Cicala's bill.2 Well done; I hope the Good God will send you the means to pay the rest; yes, my God! Your cheerfulness is a great comfort to me. If only the moment would come when the house could be filled with religious and postulants!3 Enough; let us pay everything, then lay in a few provisions, and then we'll open the door to all who want to come; enough.

2. I hope we shall soon see the light; I am close to my blood rotting; you can imagine why. What suffering! Ah, everything goes from bad to worse; God alone is for us; the... how horrible, my dear, even to think of it; enough.4

3. Today I have a fever; I cannot understand how man seeks the destruction of good, and how very little good reigns in the world. Alas! The hand of God can no longer restrain itself from striking us; everything follows the perverse world; how horrible! Pray and have others pray that I may soon.5 May all be according to his divine will. I am between the hammer and the anvil.6 Goodbye. For now I can't go on, as I still have so much to write; your

Affectionate M. R.

4. I am glad to hear the house is being put in order; for the washing you could get a woman in, who together with Rosa would be enough to do it; anyway, in a few days it will be February, and then the days will be better and longer. I hope you have received the letter in which I spoke to you at length about Poss.7

1 The letter is of 18 January.

2 She had settled a debt of L. 436 with Cigala.

3 If only the moment... postulants! That moment was not far off.

4 I hope... enough. The hope of seeing the Rules finally approved does not leave her, because the Work is God's, but she feels alone, misunderstood, alone in holding firm to the spirit of the Rules; alone while everything gets worse because men are opposed.

5 I cannot understand. A bitter observation. Pray and have others pray:

prayer is the key to graces, she is convinced of it.

6 between the marco and the anvil, between the hammer and the anvil: a vivid image that expresses graphically all the moral oppression by which she feels beaten and crushed.

7 This is L 179.

Marchioness Emilia Carrega, sister of Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega.

She often speaks of her with her sister. The Princess of Viano is coming to Genoa and it would be good for her to meet her, as well as Emilia Negrone, to whom she will write. Anna has said she would like to join her. She is to be cheerful and remember that Saint Anne wants the heart, not riches.

A.M.F.

My blessed friend,

1. I add two lines to the letter Anna is writing to the Marquis your father, first to tell you that no hours pass, when we are together with my little treasure Anna, without our speaking of you: Sr. A. Vincenza and Anna have already begun making visits; today they got a little tired; tomorrow she comes with me and we go out alone, to Cardinal Vannicelli and elsewhere.1

2. I hope to go to the Holy Father on Sunday; join us in receiving the Holy Blessing.2

3. Today the Princess of Viano came and told me she will come to Genoa next week; so we spoke of you, that you will go and see her and help her form holy acquaintances;3 Anna is already writing to your father and will tell him more; I shall also write to Emilia Negrone,4 for I should like her too to know this excellent and most noble Lady, because her Daughter-in-law will come to live in the Palace called Paradise, at Albaro; she is a most devout person and will give alms; speak to the Negrone and tell her I shall write to her.

4. My little treasure told me you would like to be with us if you had settled your affairs; my dear, what have you to settle? Are you perhaps a poor widow who must provide for her children? Perhaps your affairs would no longer have any course; come, come, listen: these are all specks of dust which, with a good shrug of the shoulders, the wind carries off; isn't that so? Enough; be cheerful and remember that Saint Anne loves to have the heart, not riches.

5. We went with Anna to the Mother President. Shall I tell you something in confidence? You know, Maria Celeste said she would gladly come with us. Imagine my allowing it! I would never do such a thing to our good Mother President; what an exchange: we poor, they rich.5

6. I'll write no more, as I want to go to bed.

Warm greetings to the Marquis your father, and receive a thousand embraces in the Heart of Jesus, in which I remain your

Most affectionate Friend Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 Anna writes; she had come to Rome in answer to the call to the Daughters of Saint Anne. To the marquis your father: Antonio Benedetto. Cardinal Vannicelli,

protector of the Institute.

2 She had the audience with the Holy Father on Sunday 1 February. Cf. L 186,2; 187,6.

3 Bice Altieri, Princess of Viano; holy acquaintances: relationships of spiritual friendship.

4 Marchioness Emilia Negrone; cf. Lettere 2, p. 705.

5 The Mother President: L 38, n. 1. Maria Celeste, perhaps one of the Oblates who, sympathetic to the FSA, had expressed a wish to join them.

She approves her writing to Genoa. She urges her to send the girls to Poss. Her plan for obtaining the Chapel furnishings is fine. Some places must be prepared in the infirmary for girls who need them. She is to send Fr Bernardo's biography to Emilia Negrone.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have received your letter and hear that my words telling you not to be upset made an impression on you;1 really, I tell you, you are originals of the first order; one doesn't know how to write to you: one way you're upset, the other way the same; really, I'd be tempted...! Enough; let's lay everything in the heart of God the Father, and our ideas will calm down;2 it's true, great patience is needed!

2. You did well to write to Genoa, as you have now done about the goods; if a misunderstanding happened once,3 there's no need at once to start making resolutions; whoever makes no mistakes never does anything. Courage — now is the time to use it; would we had more! My dear, we must become giants.

3. For charity's sake, the girls must not stay at home but go to Poss.

4. You asked me about going to the Vicar to get a chalice and chasuble.4 Go by all means; you can also go to the Ursulines for church goods. I'll send you the candlesticks from here and see whether I can find church items. Go and see Count Francesco5 and ask him to help you buy a pyx and something else; I realize you'll have little time to go out, being so busy.

5. Listen, press Accinelli to send you the man for the animals, and you'll save a great deal of expense.6

6. I would think of preparing a few beds in the house in Via della Morte for girls who fall ill, so that if they fall ill at Poss they could be taken to that infirmary, for you see it is much more convenient than ours. Isn't it? I think they now have empty beds [in the] infirmary of the Morte.7

7. Give my regards to the Canon and tell him I never forget the charity he does. Tell that person I forgot to ask him,

while I was there, kindly to give me the life of Father

Bernardo, which Emilia Negrone had begged me to get for her; I forgot completely. Get it from him and then send it to her under plain wrapper. The address: Marchioness Emilia Negrone née Centurione, that's enough. See that he gives it to you.8

8. See about the teacher for S. P. d'Arena, and for

Sestri. Ah! If only one would come to become a nun, how much we need one! From Sestri she writes that they want one there too, and are already organizing.9 How desperate; I don't know what to say; great patience is needed. If the one at the Morte became a religious, how good that would be!10 Enough; have a novena made for this to

Our Lady of the Sacred Heart, of desperate causes, that at last she may send me teachers; I hope she will, and then you'll have the means to pay the bills. Goodbye, I am your

Affectionate M. R.

1 This letter has not survived.

2 originals... tempted. You are odd ones; one doesn't know how to write to you! I'd be tempted...! As she is about to write words that might give offence, she stops.

Enough! And she seeks in the Father's heart peace for herself and her Daughters.

3 Cf. L 179, n. 4.

4 The Vicar of the Bishop of Piacenza, Mgr Francesco Tammi.

5 Count Francesco Caracciolo.

6 The man to slaughter the pigs; cf. letter of Accinelli 10.1.1874 and L 70, n. 7.

7 Extremely far-sighted, she proposes preparing in the infirmary of the house in

Via della Morte an infirmary for girls employed at the Poss factory who might fall ill.

8 Fr Tornatore was to give her the biography of Fr Bernardo Maria Clausi to send to Marchioness Negrone.

9 At Sestri they are already organizing the school. Cf. letter of Accinelli 10.1.1874.

10 If the lay teacher at the school in Via della Morte became a Daughter of Saint Anne, what an advantage!

The Mayor of Sampierdarena is expecting the Superior, so she must leave. She will come to an arrangement with the doctor under whom she will work and invite him to take on the care of the Institute's Community. She is to leave everything in order in Piacenza. After a week she will return and finish the household tasks.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received a letter from the Mayor of S. P. d'Arena asking me to send him the Superior at once. So get ready and leave with those I told you.1 When you see the Doctor, tell him you'd like him to say nothing, because it is a post you yourself wanted, and so you are better off; and commend yourself to him warmly.2

2. The Mayor tells me you are to depend on him — meaning only on the doctor — as the Municipality has so decided. I think it is a good thing for us, as this doctor is our friend. I'd like you to introduce (presentare) him to some people. I'll commend him to Federico, and meanwhile you tell the doctor so. As for the care of our house in Sampierdarena, tell him we'll do as with Albertazzi in Piacenza, and tell him the sum.3 See whether he is satisfied; he will feel more obliged.

3. For pity's sake, I commend Piacenza to you. Leave orders with Sr. A. del Buon Pastore and the Sisters; you won't (ce) tell them you are leaving for good, only for a few weeks; and you can tell her that the one at the Morte should come now and then to see the one at the Big House.4

4. In short, I think it can work very well, because all the sick girls and religious will go to the Morte;5 as for Postulants, there are none for now, and those from Genoa will stay at S. P. d'Arena.

5. Listen: as soon as you go there, take a look at that house, for I hear there are so many muddles, for charity's sake. I'm writing to the Superior now.6

6. I don't know what to do about that person's letters; I suppose I'll address them to him directly.7 I urge you to leave things as orderly as you can; it only weighs on me to think you couldn't pay all the bills. Go to the Marchioness8 and ask her for something, for charity; and see whether you can manage to pay the apothecary and the miller.

7. Go at once, and in that case do you know what I'd like? When you've been at S. P. d'Arena a week, tell them you are going to Piacenza for two days to fetch your things; so get leave for as many days as you see you can, and be at peace.9

8. Then you'll go to Poss to see how things stand, and the girls who arrive will be taken to Poss.10 Only those of the Parish Priest of the Paganina11 should have F. 50.

9. In short, my dear, leave everything well ordered. I'm sorry about the pigs. Write and tell me how you manage everything; meanwhile leave at once. Goodbye; greet all the postulants for me; send that sick one home at once.12 But leave word; send for her Mother at once. Goodbye, in haste, your

affectionate M. R.

1 I have received a letter from the Mayor: Nicolò Montano. Leave with the Sisters as I told you.

2 The doctor: no details about him are available; he was evidently the chief physician appointed to the hospital.

3 Ask him whether he is willing to take on the care of the Sampierdarena community and agree the fee, as we settled with the attending doctor of the Piacenza community, Sante Albertazzi.

4 the one at the Morte: the Superior of the house in Via della Morte, Sr. A. Filippina Bruschi, is to come and see the one at the Mother House, Sr. A. Carmelita Romainone.

5 Sick girls and religious will be admitted to the infirmary of the

House in Via della Morte; cf. L 182, n. 7.

6 that house: the Sampierdarena Institute.

7 She always enclosed her letters to Fr Tornatore in those to the Superior

Francesca.

8 Cf. L 100, n. 10.

9 After the first contacts she may ask leave to go to Piacenza and finish putting in order what she left pending.

10 Other girls were to come from Nizza and Sampierdarena to work at the Poss factory.

11 The Parish Priest Don Elia Magnani was also to place some girls there.

But these were to pay only L. 50.

12 There was a seriously ill postulant in the house.

She asks that the Institute again be granted the 50% reduction on Roman railway tickets.

Most Illustrious Director,

1. The Sisters of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne engaged in nursing the sick at home and in hospital were granted a 50% reduction on railway tickets by letter of the general management N. 6759/5934 of 5 May 73. But at the beginning of '74 this arrangement was suspended.

2. The petitioner, head of this Institute, encouraged by your kindness already experienced and driven by need, having continually to send Nurses here in Rome and the surrounding area where she has many houses, makes bold to ask you to continue your great benevolence towards this Institute by again granting this reduction. Her gratitude will know no bounds.

[MARIA ROSA GATTORNO]

She has heard the news of her father's death. She is to tell the Father and have prayers said. She urges her to leave at once and comfort her poor mother. The Mother too will go to Genoa; she is waiting for a telegram to leave.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Two telegrams reached me today, one after the other: one said papa was ill and I should leave at once; the other said papa has died. For charity's sake let that Person know and have prayers said.1

2. I want you to go soon, so you can look in on mamma and comfort her, (e) for the Superior Santina,2 if you only knew, upsets her instead of comforting her. Poor mamma! Leave at once.

3. I'm waiting for a telegram to come. I too shall come, alone with Sr. A. Eufrasina, who has done her share.3 Goodbye; I'll add nothing more, for I don't know what to say, my head is so confused. I hope you have received my letter — or rather two — and are getting ready, or have already left.4

Goodbye, yours. Have a Mass said tomorrow your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She asks first of all for prayers from Fr Tornatore and the Sisters. Sr. A. Francesca informed the Communities of Nizza, Ovada and Ferrara and asked for prayers of suffrage. (Cf. her letter of 3.1.74 to M. Rosa).

2 Santina Solenghi, of the Genoa community.

3 She was bringing Sr. A. Eufrasina Pizzoni with her from Rome.

4 L 183 speaks clearly of the departure for Sampierdarena.

She cannot understand why her letter has gone unanswered. Her tribulations are many: all that her friend foretold has come true. She has had an audience with the Holy Father and received his blessing for her too. She announces her father's death and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My most beloved,

1. I cannot understand why you have not written again, or rather answered my letter; unfortunately I found here everything you told me — alas, perhaps worse than you told me.1

2. Pray to Rosa to help me.2 Today I was at the Holy Father's audience and received it for you too.

3. Do you know that poor papa has died? Everything is needed to get up there. Write me something, for I [have] need of it.3

4. My tribulations, my dear, are numberless; blessed be God who knew how to send them to me in such abundance.

5. So far that person has not yet come about the house; pray and tell Rosa to send her to me, and my grace too.4 Ah, it is my vileness that holds back the graces God has to give.

6. I'm tired, I'm going to bed; tell me whether you have received my letter. Goodbye, it's late.

I am your affectionate friend Sr. A. R. GATTORNO

1 Cf. L 178.

2 Ibid., n. 3.

3 Cf. L 185, 1.

4 Cf. L 194,10. My grace: the approval of the Rules.
